nodes.name: Button
nodes.description: A control that performs an action when activated, such as saving, submitting a form or opening a dialog.
nodes.markdown:
A button is a control that performs an action when activated, such as saving a record, submitting a form or opening a [modal dialog](node:Modal%20dialog). Use the native `<button>` element. It receives keyboard focus, activates on Enter and Space, and is announced as a button by screen readers, the software that reads an interface aloud. A `<div>` with a click handler has none of this, which is why some controls work with a mouse and do nothing from the keyboard.

The nearest alternative is a link, and the choice depends on what happens next.

| Element     | Use it when                                    | Activates with |
| ----------- | ---------------------------------------------- | -------------- |
| `<button>`  | The action changes this page or sends data     | Enter, Space   |
| `<a href>`  | The action goes to another URL                 | Enter          |

A link styled to look like a button should stay a link, because users expect to open it in a new tab or copy its address.

A common bug comes from the default type. Inside a `<form>`, a `<button>` with no `type` attribute is a submit button. A "Cancel" or "Show password" button then submits the form and can reload the page, losing what the user typed. Set the type on every button.

```html
<button type="button">Cancel</button>
<button type="submit">Save invoice</button>
```

The accessible name, which is the text a screen reader announces, comes from the button's content. Prefer a specific label such as "Delete invoice" over "Click here". After activation, focus should land somewhere sensible. If the button opens a dialog, focus moves inside it.

The native `disabled` attribute removes a button from the Tab order, so keyboard users may never discover it. `aria-disabled="true"` keeps it focusable, but your script must then block the action. See [disabled state](node:Disabled%20state) for that trade-off, and [touch target](node:Touch%20target) for minimum sizes.
quotes: The cancel button on the settings form keeps saving people's changes.
It has no `type`, so it defaults to submit. Add `type="button"`.

nodes.name: Icon button
nodes.description: A button that shows a symbol with no visible text, and needs a separate accessible name to make sense to assistive technology.
nodes.markdown:
An icon [button](node:Button) is a button that shows a symbol and no visible text, such as a bin for delete or a cross for close. It saves space in dense interfaces such as a [toolbar](node:Toolbar) or a table row. Use one only when the symbol is widely understood. If people would have to guess, use a text label or put a visible word beside the icon.

The usual failure is a missing name. With no text inside, a screen reader (software that reads the interface aloud) may announce only "button", so the user cannot tell whether it deletes, closes or shares. Provide the name with `aria-label` or visually hidden text, and hide the decorative graphic.

```html
<button type="button" aria-label="Delete invoice 1042">
  <svg aria-hidden="true" viewBox="0 0 24 24">...</svg>
</button>
```

Names in repeated rows should say which item they act on. Twenty controls all called "Delete" are hard to tell apart when listed by a screen reader.

Keyboard behaviour matches any button: Tab reaches it, and Enter or Space activates it. Inside a toolbar, arrow keys move between controls instead.

A [tooltip](node:Tooltip) helps sighted users learn what the symbol means, and it must appear on keyboard focus as well as hover. It does not replace the accessible name. If the tooltip repeats that name, do not also attach it with `aria-describedby`, or the same words are announced twice.

| Concern     | What to check                                                       |
| ----------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Target size | At least 24 by 24 CSS pixels (WCAG 2.5.8), unless an exception applies |
| Contrast    | Icon at 3:1 against adjacent colours (WCAG 1.4.11)                  |
| State       | Use a [toggle button](node:Toggle%20button) for on and off          |

A small glyph can sit inside a larger clickable area, so padding is the usual way to reach the [touch target](node:Touch%20target) size.
quotes: VoiceOver just says 'button' for every action in this table row.
They're icon buttons with no names. Add an `aria-label` that includes the invoice number.

nodes.name: Toggle button
nodes.description: A button with a pressed and an unpressed state, used for on-off commands such as Bold or Mute.
nodes.markdown:
A toggle [button](node:Button) is a button with two states, pressed and not pressed, such as Bold in a text editor or Mute in a video player. HTML has no dedicated element for it. Use a native `<button>` and expose the state with `aria-pressed`.

```html
<button type="button" aria-pressed="false">Mute</button>
```

Enter and Space flip the state, and focus stays on the control. A screen reader (software that reads the interface aloud) announces something like "Mute, toggle button, not pressed". Styling from the attribute, with `[aria-pressed="true"]`, keeps the visual state and the exposed state from drifting apart.

There are two valid ways to communicate the state, and mixing them is the common bug.

| Approach      | Label               | State attribute      | User hears              |
| ------------- | ------------------- | -------------------- | ----------------------- |
| Pressed state | Stays "Mute"        | `aria-pressed`       | "Mute, pressed"         |
| Label change  | "Mute" to "Unmute"  | None                 | "Unmute, button"        |

If the label changes and `aria-pressed` is also set, the user can hear "Unmute, pressed" and has no way to tell whether the sound is on. The WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices state that the label on a toggle must not change when its state changes. Pick one approach per control.

Choose the nearest alternative by what the control means. A toggle button suits a command in a [toolbar](node:Toolbar) that applies to the current content. A [switch](node:Switch) suits a setting that is on or off, such as email alerts. A [checkbox](node:Checkbox) suits a choice that is submitted later with a form. For one choice among several, use a [segmented control](node:Segmented%20control).

The pressed look must not rely on colour alone (WCAG 1.4.1). A filled background, border or icon change is easier to perceive, particularly when two neighbouring toggles are in different states.
quotes: The screen reader says 'Unmute, pressed'. Is the audio on or off?
We're swapping the label and setting `aria-pressed`. Keep the label as 'Mute' and only change the state.

nodes.name: Split button
nodes.description: A primary action joined to a small arrow that opens a menu of related alternatives.
nodes.markdown:
A split [button](node:Button) is two controls drawn as one: a main button that runs the default action, and a narrow arrow button that opens a list of related actions. A "Merge" control with "Squash and merge" and "Rebase and merge" behind the arrow is a typical example. Use it when one action is clearly the common choice and the others are variations of it. If no option is the default, a plain [dropdown menu](node:Dropdown%20menu) is clearer. The WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices have no dedicated split button pattern, so build it from two patterns they do define. ```html
``` | Part | Role | Keyboard | | ----------- | ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------ | | Main action | `button` | Enter or Space runs the default action | | Arrow | Menu button | Enter, Space or Down Arrow opens the menu | | Open menu | `menu` | Arrows move, Enter activates, Escape closes | Each half is its own Tab stop unless the pair sits inside a [toolbar](node:Toolbar). When the menu closes with Escape, focus returns to the arrow. A common structural bug is nesting the arrow inside the main button. HTML does not allow interactive content inside a `
quotes: Clicking the little arrow also fires the deploy.
The arrow is nested inside the main button. Split the button into two siblings so the click only opens the menu.

nodes.name: Segmented control
nodes.description: A row of joined options where one is active, used to choose a view or value from a small set.
nodes.markdown:
A segmented control is a row of joined options where one is active, such as Day, Week and Month on a calendar. It keeps every choice visible and changes with one click. Use it for a small set of short labels. For a long list, or labels that do not fit, a [select](node:Select) is a better fit.

The look does not define the semantics, and ARIA, the attributes that describe controls to assistive technology, has no segmented control role. Decide what the control does, then use the matching pattern.

| What it does                  | Build it as                      | Keyboard                           |
| ----------------------------- | -------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| Sets a value                  | [Radio group](node:Radio%20group) | Arrows move and choose            |
| Shows a different panel       | [Tabs](node:Tabs)                | Arrows move between tabs           |
| Turns options on independently | [Toggle buttons](node:Toggle%20button) | Tab, then Enter or Space     |

For the value case, native radio inputs provide the behaviour without scripting. Hide the circle visually and style the label.

```html
<fieldset class="segmented">
  <legend>Calendar view</legend>
  <label><input type="radio" name="view" value="day" /> Day</label>
  <label><input type="radio" name="view" value="week" checked /> Week</label>
  <label><input type="radio" name="view" value="month" /> Month</label>
</fieldset>
```

The common way this breaks is hiding the inputs with `display: none`. That removes them from the keyboard and the accessibility tree, so the control works only with a mouse. Clip them visually or set `opacity: 0` on an input that stays in the layout, and show focus on the label with `:has(:focus-visible)`.

Two other problems recur. The active segment is often marked by a subtle tint alone, which fails WCAG 1.4.1 if colour is the only cue. Labels can also overflow when the page is zoomed, because the row cannot wrap. WCAG 1.4.10 expects content to reflow at a width of 320 CSS pixels, so let the segments wrap or change to a select at a narrow [breakpoint](node:Breakpoint).
quotes: I can't reach the Week and Month options with the keyboard.
The radios are `display: none` in the segmented control. Hide them visually instead so they stay focusable.

nodes.name: Floating action button
nodes.description: A prominent round button fixed above the content, usually in a bottom corner, for a screen's main action.
nodes.markdown:
A floating action [button](node:Button), often shortened to FAB, is a prominent button fixed above the content, usually in a bottom corner of a mobile screen. It holds the main action on that screen, such as composing a message. Use it when one action dominates and the user needs it at any scroll position. If a screen has several equal actions, or the action fits in the page header or a [toolbar](node:Toolbar), an ordinary button is simpler.

The FAB has no special role. Build it as a native `<button>` with an accessible name, since most FABs show only an icon. Tab reaches it, and Enter or Space activates it.

```css
.fab {
  position: fixed;
  inset-block-end: calc(16px + env(safe-area-inset-bottom));
  inset-inline-end: 16px;
}
```

The common failure is covering content. The last row of a list ends up under the button, so its menu or link cannot be tapped. Reserve space at the end of the scrolling content and account for the device [safe area](node:Safe%20area).

The same overlap affects keyboard users. WCAG 2.4.11 requires that a focused element is not entirely hidden by author-created content, and a fixed button can hide one as the page scrolls to it. Setting `scroll-padding-block-end` on the scroll container keeps focused items clear.

| Problem                         | Fix                                        |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| Last list item is covered       | Add bottom padding to the list             |
| Focused element sits underneath | Use `scroll-padding-block-end`             |
| Clashes with tab bar            | Offset it above [bottom navigation](node:Bottom%20navigation) |

Fixed positioning changes where the button appears, but not its place in the Tab order, which follows the DOM. A FAB at the end of the markup is reached last.

If the button expands into several actions, treat it as a menu button with `aria-haspopup="menu"` and `aria-expanded`, and follow the [dropdown menu](node:Dropdown%20menu) keyboard behaviour.
quotes: I can't tap the kebab menu on the last row. The compose button is on top of it.
The FAB overlaps the list end. Add bottom padding to the list that matches its height.

nodes.name: Toolbar
nodes.description: A labelled group of related controls that takes one Tab stop and uses arrow keys to move between them.
nodes.markdown:
A toolbar is a labelled group of related controls, such as the formatting row above a [rich text editor](node:Rich%20text%20editor). In the ARIA sense, using `role="toolbar"`, the whole group takes a single Tab stop and arrow keys move between its controls. This keeps a keyboard user from pressing Tab twenty times to get past a row of formatting commands. The WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices recommend the role only for groups of three or more controls. For a pair of [buttons](node:Button), or a row of unrelated actions, use a plain container or `role="group"` and leave each one as a normal Tab stop. | Key | Action in a horizontal toolbar | | ----------------- | -------------------------------------------- | | Tab, Shift+Tab | Move focus into or out of the toolbar | | Right, Left Arrow | Move to the next or previous control | | Home, End | Optionally move to the first or last control | | Enter, Space | Activate the focused control | In a vertical toolbar, set `aria-orientation="vertical"`, and Up and Down Arrow do the moving. Wrapping from the last control to the first is optional. ```html
``` The single Tab stop is usually built with a [roving tabindex](node:Roving%20tabindex), where one control has `tabindex="0"` and the rest have `-1`. On first entry, focus goes to the first enabled control. On return, it can go back to the last one used. The common bug is adding the role without the keyboard behaviour. A screen reader then announces a toolbar, but arrow keys do nothing. The reverse problem comes from controls that need the same arrow keys, such as a text input or [slider](node:Slider) in a horizontal toolbar. Avoid them, or include only one and place it last. Disabled controls are usually skipped, but can stay focusable when users need to discover them.
quotes: Tabbing through the editor takes forever because every format button is a stop.
Make it a real toolbar with one Tab stop and arrow keys between the buttons.

nodes.name: Text field
nodes.description: A single-line input for short typed values such as a name, email address or phone number.
nodes.markdown:
A text field is a single-line input for short typed values, such as a name, email address or phone number. Use the native `<input>` element with a visible `<label>`. For content that may run over several lines, use a [textarea](node:Textarea). When the value must come from a known list, use a [select](node:Select) or [combobox](node:Combobox).

The `type` attribute changes the on-screen keyboard and the validation the browser performs, while the field looks much the same.

| Value      | Use for             | Effect                                     |
| ---------- | ------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| `text`     | General short text  | No format check                            |
| `email`    | Email addresses     | Format check, keyboard with `@`            |
| `tel`      | Phone numbers       | Phone keypad, no format check              |
| `url`      | Web addresses       | Format check, URL keyboard                 |
| `password` | Secrets             | Masks characters                           |

```html
<label for="email">Work email</label>
<input id="email" name="email" type="email" autocomplete="email" />
```

The `autocomplete` attribute tells browsers and password managers what the field holds, so they can fill it in. WCAG 1.3.5 expects this on fields that collect information about the user.

A common failure is using a placeholder as the label. The text disappears as soon as the user starts typing, so anyone who pauses or returns to check the field cannot tell what it asks for. A placeholder may add an example, but the label should stay visible. The [form field](node:Form%20field) entry covers how the label, hint and error fit together.

A native input needs no keyboard work: Tab focuses it, and arrows, Home and End move the caret. Pressing Enter usually submits the surrounding form.

Use `readonly` when a value should be visible, focusable and submitted but not edited. A `disabled` field is skipped by Tab and is not submitted. Blocking paste makes entry harder, especially for people using password managers, so leave it enabled.
quotes: Users keep emailing to ask what the second box on the signup form is for.
Its only label is a placeholder, so it vanishes on typing. Give the text field a real label.

nodes.name: Textarea
nodes.description: A multi-line plain text input for longer content such as comments, messages and descriptions.
nodes.markdown:
A textarea is a multi-line plain text input for longer content such as comments, messages and descriptions. Use the native `<textarea>` with a visible `<label>`. For a short single value, use a [text field](node:Text%20field). If people need headings, links or bold, use a [rich text editor](node:Rich%20text%20editor).

Initial content goes between the tags rather than in a `value` attribute, and any whitespace there becomes part of the value. Indenting the closing tag in a template is a common reason a textarea appears to start with stray spaces.

```html
<label for="note">Delivery note</label>
<textarea id="note" name="note" rows="4" maxlength="500"></textarea>
```

| Attribute or property   | Effect                                                     |
| ----------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `rows`                  | Visible lines. Defaults to 2                               |
| `cols`                  | Visible width in average characters. Defaults to 20        |
| `maxlength`             | Limit in UTF-16 code units                                 |
| `wrap="hard"`           | Inserts line breaks on submit. Requires `cols`             |
| `resize` (CSS)          | Controls the drag handle                                   |

Character limits are a frequent source of bugs. `maxlength` counts UTF-16 code units, so many emoji count as two. Line breaks are normalised to two characters on submission, so a value that fits the counter in the browser can exceed a server limit. Pasted text can also be cut off at the limit with no message. Show a live count, validate on the server using the same counting rule, and tell the user when text was trimmed.

Enter inserts a new line and Tab moves focus to the next control. Do not intercept Tab to insert indentation unless the user has a documented way to leave, because WCAG 2.1.2 forbids keyboard traps.

Removing the resize handle takes away a control people use to read their own text. For auto-growing fields, MDN lists `field-sizing: content` as newly available across current browsers since June 2026. Older browsers ignore it, so keep a sensible `rows` value.
quotes: The form says 500 characters left, but the API rejects it as too long.
The textarea counts a newline as one and the submitted value counts it as two. Match the server's rule.

nodes.name: Checkbox
nodes.description: A control for an independent yes-or-no choice, or for choosing any number of options from a group.
nodes.markdown:
A checkbox is a control for an independent yes-or-no choice, or for choosing any number of options from a group. Use the native `<input type="checkbox">` with a `<label>`. Clicking the label toggles the box, which gives a larger target for free.

| Control                       | Choices                  | Takes effect          |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------------ | --------------------- |
| Checkbox                      | Zero, one or many        | Usually on form submit |
| [Radio group](node:Radio%20group) | Exactly one          | Usually on form submit |
| [Switch](node:Switch)         | On or off                | Immediately           |

Space toggles a focused checkbox. Enter does not, and in a form it may submit instead. Each box is its own Tab stop. Screen readers (software that reads the interface aloud) announce the label, the role and whether it is checked.

```html
<fieldset>
  <legend>Notify me about</legend>
  <label><input type="checkbox" name="notify" value="invoices" /> Invoices</label>
  <label><input type="checkbox" name="notify" value="reports" /> Reports</label>
</fieldset>
```

Wrap related boxes in a `<fieldset>` with a `<legend>`, so the group's question is available alongside each option.

An unchecked checkbox sends nothing on submission, so the server receives no field at all rather than `false`. An update handler that only writes fields it receives will leave the old value in place, and the user's "off" never saves. Treat a missing field as false, or send the state explicitly. Several boxes sharing a `name` send one pair each, so the server must read all values and not just the last.

A parent checkbox for a group can show a third, partly checked state. Set it from script with `input.indeterminate = true`, as no HTML attribute exists for it. The property is visual and has no effect on submission, which depends only on `checked`. For custom controls, the equivalent is `aria-checked="mixed"`.

If you restyle the box, keep the real input in place and visually hidden. Using `display: none` removes it from the keyboard.
quotes: People untick marketing emails, save, and it comes back ticked.
An unchecked checkbox isn't submitted, so our update skips the field. Treat missing as false.

nodes.name: Radio group
nodes.description: A set of options where exactly one can be chosen, with arrow keys moving the choice inside a single Tab stop.
nodes.markdown:
A radio group is a set of options where only one can be chosen at a time, such as a delivery speed. All options stay visible, so people can compare them before deciding. Build it from native `<input type="radio">` elements that share a `name`, wrapped in a `<fieldset>` with a `<legend>` that states the question.

```html
<fieldset>
  <legend>Delivery speed</legend>
  <label><input type="radio" name="speed" value="standard" checked /> Standard</label>
  <label><input type="radio" name="speed" value="express" /> Express</label>
</fieldset>
```

The group behaves as one Tab stop, and the arrow keys change the choice.

| Key               | Behaviour                                                 |
| ----------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| Tab               | Enters the group at the checked option, or the first one  |
| Down, Right Arrow | Moves to the next option and checks it, wrapping at the end |
| Up, Left Arrow    | Moves to the previous option and checks it, wrapping      |
| Space             | Checks the focused option if it is unchecked              |

Because arrow keys change the value as they move, a handler that acts on every change breaks keyboard use. If choosing an option reloads results or navigates away, a keyboard user cannot get past the first option. WCAG 3.2.2 says changing a setting must not cause a change of context without warning. Apply the choice with a separate [button](node:Button), or limit the change to updating content nearby.

Once a radio is checked, a user cannot uncheck it by clicking it again. An optional question therefore needs an explicit "None" option. If nothing is checked, the group is left out of the submitted data entirely, and `required` on any radio in the group makes one choice mandatory.

Compared with its alternatives, a radio group suits a short list that benefits from being read in full. A [select](node:Select) takes less room for a long list. A [checkbox](node:Checkbox) group is for choosing several, and a [segmented control](node:Segmented%20control) is a compact visual treatment of the same single choice.
quotes: With the keyboard, pressing Down on the sort options reloads the page every time.
The radio group submits on change. Add an Apply button so arrow keys can move freely.

nodes.name: Switch
nodes.description: An on-off control for a setting that takes effect immediately, without a separate save step.
nodes.markdown:
A switch is an on-off control for a setting that takes effect immediately, such as turning on email alerts. People expect the change to apply at once. The usual confusion comes from placing one inside a form with a Save [button](node:Button): the user flips it, leaves the page, and the setting was never stored. If a choice applies only on submit, use a [checkbox](node:Checkbox).

| Control                              | Meaning                 | Applies              |
| ------------------------------------ | ----------------------- | -------------------- |
| Switch                               | A setting is on or off  | Immediately          |
| Checkbox                             | An option is chosen     | Usually on submit    |
| [Toggle button](node:Toggle%20button) | A command is active    | Immediately          |

The simplest robust build is a native checkbox with the `switch` role. It keeps focus, form and label behaviour, and assistive technology announces it as a switch.

```html
<label>
  <input type="checkbox" role="switch" name="alerts" checked />
  Email alerts
</label>
```

HTML also has a newer `switch` attribute on checkbox inputs. MDN describes it as experimental with limited support, and browsers without support ignore it and show a normal checkbox.

Space toggles a focused switch. The WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices list Enter as optional, and a native checkbox does not toggle on Enter. A custom element needs `role="switch"`, `aria-checked`, `tabindex="0"` and its own key handling.

Keep the label constant. "Email alerts, on" is clear, whereas a label that changes to "Email alerts disabled" can be announced as "Email alerts disabled, on". The state also needs more than a colour change to satisfy WCAG 1.4.1, so use thumb position, an icon or on and off text.

Because a switch applies at once, the save can fail after the thumb has already moved. Show a pending state if the request is slow. On failure, move the switch back and report the error in text, for example with a [toast](node:Toast), so the display does not claim a setting that was not saved.
quotes: I turned off alerts, but I'm still getting emails.
The switch only updates local state until you press Save. Either persist it on change or use a checkbox.

nodes.name: Select
nodes.description: A native control that opens a list of predefined options and shows the chosen one when closed.
nodes.markdown:
A select is a control that opens a list of predefined options and shows the chosen one when closed, such as a country picker. Use the native `<select>` element whenever it fits. It comes with keyboard support, type-ahead and the operating system's picker on phones, all of which a custom replacement has to rebuild.

```html
<label for="country">Country</label>
<select id="country" name="country" required>
  <option value="">Choose a country</option>
  <optgroup label="Europe">
    <option value="fr">France</option>
    <option value="de">Germany</option>
  </optgroup>
</select>
```

The empty first option makes `required` work: if the user leaves it, the form reports the field as missing. Without it, the first real option is submitted silently, so a form can collect a default country nobody chose.

| Situation                         | Use                                   |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- |
| A few options worth comparing     | [Radio group](node:Radio%20group)     |
| A longer fixed list               | Select                                |
| Hundreds of options, or typing helps | [Combobox](node:Combobox)             |
| Several values allowed            | [Multi-select](node:Multi-select)     |
| A list of actions, not values     | [Dropdown menu](node:Dropdown%20menu) |

A single-choice dropdown is exposed to assistive technology with the `combobox` role, and a list with `size` above 1 or the `multiple` attribute is exposed as `listbox`. Exact key behaviour varies by browser and platform. In general, Tab focuses it, arrow keys or Space work with the list, and typing jumps to a matching option.

A select that navigates or submits as soon as its value changes can break keyboard use. On some browsers, arrowing through options fires a change for each one, so keyboard users are sent away on the first press. WCAG 3.2.2 requires advance warning for this kind of context change, so use a submit [button](node:Button) instead.

Styling has been the main reason teams replace the element. Customizable select, enabled with `appearance: base-select`, allows full styling of the button and picker. MDN lists it as limited availability, but unsupported browsers fall back to a standard select, so it works as an enhancement.
quotes: Why do so many signups list Afghanistan?
The select defaults to the first country. Add an empty option and mark the field required.

nodes.name: Combobox
nodes.description: An input paired with a popup of suggestions, letting people type to filter and choose a value from a long list.
nodes.markdown:
A combobox is an input paired with a popup of suggestions, so people can type to filter a long list and then choose a value. City and assignee pickers are common examples. Choose it over a [select](node:Select) when the list is too long to scan. If the value is free text with occasional hints, the native `` is simpler, although its popup cannot be styled and some screen reader and browser pairings do not announce it. The WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices define two kinds. An editable combobox accepts typing, and a select-only combobox behaves like a custom select with no text entry. In both, DOM focus stays on the input while `aria-activedescendant` points to the highlighted option, so the user can keep typing. ```html
  • Paris
  • Porto
``` | Key | Action | | --------------- | --------------------------------------------------- | | Down Arrow | Opens the popup or moves to the next option | | Up Arrow | Optionally moves to the previous or last option | | Enter | Accepts the highlighted option | | Escape | Closes the popup, and may then clear the input | | Alt+Down Arrow | Optionally opens the popup without moving into it | | Tab | Leaves the field. The popup is not a Tab stop | Several failures recur. Enter can submit the surrounding form while the popup is open, because the handler did not prevent the default. `aria-expanded` may stay `false` after opening, so screen readers never report the list. Filtering may change the options without announcing anything, so add a `role="status"` message such as "4 results", which WCAG 4.1.3 expects for this kind of update. Async options add a race: a slow response for "pa" can arrive after the one for "par" and replace it. Discard stale responses. Decide also what happens to text that matches no option when focus leaves, since keeping it silently can submit an invalid value.
quotes: Pressing Enter on a suggestion submits the whole form.
The combobox isn't preventing the default. Enter should accept the option while the popup is open.

nodes.name: Multi-select
nodes.description: A control for choosing any number of values from a known list of options.
nodes.markdown:
A multi-[select](node:Select) is a control for choosing any number of values from a known list, such as assigning several labels to a ticket. Pick a form based on how long the list is and how much room you have.

| Form                               | Fits                     | Trade-off                              |
| ---------------------------------- | ------------------------ | -------------------------------------- |
| [Checkbox](node:Checkbox) group    | Short lists              | Takes vertical space                   |
| `<select multiple>`                | Basic internal tools     | Modifier keys are hard to discover     |
| Listbox with `aria-multiselectable` | Custom scrolling lists  | You build all keyboard behaviour       |
| [Combobox](node:Combobox) with [chips](node:Chip) | Long, searchable lists | Most complex to build                  |

If people need to add values that are not in the list, use a [tag input](node:Tag%20input).

The native `<select multiple>` has a well-known trap. A plain click replaces the whole selection, so someone carefully choosing items with Ctrl or Command can lose them all with one unmodified click. MDN notes that its keyboard mechanisms are not standardised and differ across browsers and operating systems.

For a custom listbox, the WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices recommend a model where moving focus does not change the selection.

| Key                | Action                                    |
| ------------------ | ----------------------------------------- |
| Up, Down Arrow     | Move focus                                |
| Space              | Toggle the focused option                 |
| Shift+Space        | Optionally select a contiguous range      |
| Ctrl+A             | Optionally select or clear all            |

Mark options with `aria-selected` or `aria-checked`, not both, and use the same one across the product. Keep the popup open after each choice so people can pick several in a row.

Filtering causes a recurring problem: chosen items vanish from the list when the search text no longer matches them, and users think their picks were lost. Show the current selection outside the filtered list.

On submission, each value is sent as its own pair, such as `label=bug&label=urgent`. A server that reads only one value will silently keep just the last one.
quotes: I picked eight labels, clicked one more, and the other eight disappeared.
That's the native multi-select needing Ctrl. Replace it with a checkbox list.

nodes.name: Tag input
nodes.description: A text input that turns each entered value into a removable tag, for free-form lists such as labels or email recipients.
nodes.markdown:
A tag input is a text input that turns each entered value into a removable item, such as labels on an article or recipients in an email. Each item is usually drawn as a [chip](node:Chip) inside the field. Use it when people can add values of their own. If the values must come from a fixed list, a [multi-select](node:Multi-select) prevents typos and duplicates. The WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices have no tag input pattern, so the behaviour below is convention built from native parts. A simple structure is a list of tags, each with a real remove [button](node:Button), followed by a labelled text input. ```html
  • design

Press Enter or comma to add a label.

``` | Key or action | Common behaviour | | --------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- | | Enter or comma | Commits the typed text as a tag | | Backspace, empty input | Focuses or removes the last tag | | Tab | Moves on, and should commit or keep pending text | | Paste | Splits a list into separate tags | Enter may submit the surrounding form instead of adding the tag, so prevent the default only when there is text to commit. Text left in the input when the user tabs away can be lost silently. Backspace that deletes a tag at once is easy to trigger by accident, so many implementations focus the tag on the first press and remove it on the second. Input method editors, used to compose characters in languages such as Chinese and Japanese, also use Enter to confirm text. A handler that ignores this creates a broken tag mid-word. Check `event.isComposing` before committing. When a tag is removed, its button disappears and focus would fall to the page body. Move focus to the next tag or back to the input. Announce additions and removals through a `role="status"` region, since nothing else tells a screen reader user the list changed.
quotes: Japanese users get half-finished tags every time they confirm a word.
Enter is committing during IME composition. Have the tag input check `isComposing` first.

nodes.name: Number input
nodes.description: A field for numeric quantities, with step controls and range limits, and a poor fit for digit strings such as card numbers.
nodes.markdown:
A number input is a field for numeric quantities, such as how many tickets to buy. The native `<input type="number">` validates the entry, supports `min`, `max` and `step`, and is exposed to assistive technology with the `spinbutton` role. Use it for values where adding or subtracting one makes sense. For an approximate value, use a [slider](node:Slider).

Many values that contain digits are not numbers. Card numbers, postal codes, phone numbers and one-time codes should not use it, because arrow keys can change them and leading zeros have no numeric meaning. For these, use a [text field](node:Text%20field) with `inputmode`.

| Value              | Markup                                            |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------- |
| Quantity           | `type="number" min="1" step="1"`                  |
| Price              | `type="text" inputmode="decimal"`                 |
| Postal code        | `type="text" autocomplete="postal-code"`          |
| Numeric PIN        | `type="text" inputmode="numeric"`                 |

The default `step` is 1, so a value of `1.5` is invalid unless you set `step="0.5"` or `step="any"`. This is a frequent reason a form refuses a price that looks correct. When the typed text is not a valid number, the input's `.value` is typically an empty string, so code can read a blank where the user can see text. Check `input.validity.badInput` to tell the two apart.

For a custom control, the WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices define these keys for the `spinbutton` role.

| Key                  | Action                                  |
| -------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| Up, Down Arrow       | Increase or decrease by one step        |
| Page Up, Page Down   | Optionally change by a larger step      |
| Home, End            | Go to the minimum or maximum, if known  |

Focus stays in the text field, and increment [buttons](node:Button) are usually left out of the Tab order because the arrow keys do the same job. Set `aria-valuenow`, `aria-valuemin` and `aria-valuemax`, and `aria-invalid="true"` when the value is out of range.
quotes: The price field rejects 19.99 with a 'nearest valid value' error.
That number input has the default step of 1. Set `step="0.01"`, or use text with `inputmode="decimal"`.

nodes.name: Slider
nodes.description: A control for choosing a value along a range by moving a thumb, suited to approximate values such as volume.
nodes.markdown:
A slider is a control for choosing a value along a range by moving a thumb, such as volume or brightness. It suits values where the approximate position matters more than the exact figure. If people need a specific value, such as a price of 149, use a [number input](node:Number%20input), or pair the two so either can set the value.

Use the native `<input type="range">`, which has the `slider` role and built-in keyboard support. It defaults to a range of 0 to 100 with a starting value halfway along, so an untouched slider can submit 50 as if the user chose it.

```html
<label for="volume">Volume</label>
<input id="volume" type="range" min="0" max="10" step="1" value="4" />
```

| Key                | Action                            |
| ------------------ | --------------------------------- |
| Right, Up Arrow    | Increase by one step              |
| Left, Down Arrow   | Decrease by one step              |
| Home, End          | Go to the minimum or maximum      |
| Page Up, Page Down | Optionally move by a larger step  |

When the raw number means little, set `aria-valuetext` so a screen reader (software that reads the interface aloud) announces something useful, such as "Medium" or "£40" rather than "2". Also show the current value on screen.

WCAG 2.5.7 requires a single-pointer alternative to dragging. Letting users click or tap the track satisfies it. Native sliders generally do this, and custom ones often do not.

A range slider with two thumbs needs two focusable elements. Each is its own Tab stop, and the Tab order stays fixed even if the thumbs swap visual position. When one thumb limits the other, update the dependent `aria-valuemin` or `aria-valuemax` as it moves.

Firing a request on every `input` event makes dragging stutter. Update the display on `input` and fetch on `change`. Some touch screen readers may not operate custom sliders, so test on real devices.
quotes: The price filter refetches on every pixel of drag, and the page locks up.
The slider is wired to `input`. Update the label there and run the query on `change`.

nodes.name: Date picker
nodes.description: A control for entering a calendar date by typing or by choosing from a month grid.
nodes.markdown:
A date picker is a control for entering a calendar date, by typing or by choosing from a month grid. The native `<input type="date">` handles locale display, a built-in picker and range limits. Its appearance varies by browser, but it is the first option to try.

```html
<label for="start">Start date</label>
<input id="start" type="date" min="2026-01-01" max="2026-12-31" />
```

The displayed format follows the user's locale, while `value` is always `yyyy-mm-dd`. A common bug comes from parsing it with `new Date("2026-03-01")`. JavaScript treats a date-only string as midnight UTC, so a user west of UTC sees 28 February. Keep calendar dates as plain strings unless a time zone is part of the meaning.

For a date of birth, paging back decades is slow, so a typed field or separate day, month and year inputs work better. For a date close to today, a calendar helps people see weekdays. In any custom picker, keep a typed input available too.

A custom calendar usually opens in a [modal dialog](node:Modal%20dialog) with a grid of days. The WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices example uses these keys.

| Key                  | Action in the grid                        |
| -------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| Arrow keys           | Previous or next day, or same day by week |
| Home, End            | First or last day of the week             |
| Page Up, Page Down   | Previous or next month                    |
| Shift+Page Up, Down  | Same month in previous or next year       |
| Enter, Space         | Choose the date and close                 |
| Escape               | Close without choosing                    |

Only one day is in the Tab order at a time, using a [roving tabindex](node:Roving%20tabindex). The chosen day has `aria-selected="true"`, and today can use `aria-current="date"`. The month heading should be a polite live region so that paging is announced.

After choosing, focus returns to the trigger.
quotes: Customers in New York book March 1st, and the confirmation says February 28th.
The date picker value is parsed as UTC. Keep it as a plain date string.

nodes.name: File upload
nodes.description: A control for choosing files from a device and sending them, often with a drop zone, progress and per-file errors.
nodes.markdown:
A file upload is a control for choosing files from a device and sending them to a server. The native `<input type="file">` opens the system file picker, works from the keyboard, and on phones can offer the camera. A custom drop zone is an addition to this control and should not replace it.

```html
<label for="receipts">Upload receipts (PDF or JPEG)</label>
<input id="receipts" type="file" name="receipts"
       accept=".pdf,image/jpeg" multiple />
```

The `accept` attribute is only a hint to the file picker. Users can usually override it, so a wrong file type can still arrive. Check type and size in the browser for quick feedback, and validate again on the server, which is the only check that can be trusted.

| Stage    | What the interface does                                |
| -------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| Choose   | Picker or drop, with accepted types and limits stated  |
| Check    | Reject wrong type or size with a specific message      |
| Upload   | Show a [progress bar](node:Progress%20bar) per file    |
| Finish   | List the file name with a remove [button](node:Button) |
| Fail     | Keep the file listed, with the reason and a retry      |

A dropzone built only on [drag and drop](node:Drag%20and%20drop) excludes keyboard users and anyone who cannot drag. WCAG 2.5.7 requires a single-pointer alternative to dragging, and a visible "Choose files" control provides it.

Styled upload controls often break because the real input is hidden with `display: none`, which takes it out of the Tab order. Keep it visually hidden but focusable, or use a real button that calls `input.click()`.

Choosing the same file twice does nothing by default. The `change` event does not fire because the value did not change. Clear it after handling with `input.value = ""`.

Announce progress milestones and results through a `role="status"` region, so that screen reader users know when the upload ends.
quotes: If an upload fails and I pick the same file again, nothing happens.
The file upload input keeps its old value, so `change` doesn't fire. Reset it after each attempt.

nodes.name: OTP input
nodes.description: A field for a short one-time passcode sent by SMS, email or an authenticator app during sign-in.
nodes.markdown:
An OTP input is a field for a one-time passcode, the short code sent by SMS, email or an authenticator app during sign-in. Designs often show it as six separate boxes. The more robust build is one input styled to look like boxes, because a single field handles paste, autofill and deletion without any script.

```html
<label for="code">Verification code</label>
<input id="code" name="code" type="text" inputmode="numeric"
       autocomplete="one-time-code" maxlength="6" />
```

| Attribute                       | Purpose                                     |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| `autocomplete="one-time-code"`  | Lets the browser or OS offer the code       |
| `inputmode="numeric"`           | Shows a digit keyboard without number rules |
| `type="text"`                   | Keeps leading zeros                         |
| `maxlength`                     | Limits entry to the code length             |

Do not use `type="number"`. A [number input](node:Number%20input) has no use for leading zeros, and its arrow keys can change the code. If a code may contain letters, drop `inputmode`.

Split boxes commonly break paste. The user copies 482913, pastes, and only the 4 appears, because the first box accepts a single character. The Understanding document for WCAG 3.3.8, Accessible Authentication (Minimum), says a code field must allow pasting or automatic filling, and calls out split fields that take only one digit on paste.

If the design requires separate boxes, each needs a label such as "Digit 3 of 6", the group needs a name, paste must spread across all boxes, and Backspace in an empty box must move to the previous one. Screen reader users then hear six fields instead of one, which is the main reason to prefer the single input.

Submitting automatically on the last digit can fail WCAG 3.2.2 unless users are told in advance, and it gives no chance to correct a mistake. Keep a visible Verify [button](node:Button).

Codes expire, so state how long one lasts, offer a resend option, and report wrong or expired codes in text beside the field.
quotes: Pasting the code from my password manager only fills the first box.
The OTP input is six separate fields. Switch to one field with `autocomplete="one-time-code"`.

nodes.name: Search field
nodes.description: A text input for entering a query, usually inside a search landmark, that filters content or returns results.
nodes.markdown:
A search field is a text input for entering a query that filters the current page or returns results. Use `<input type="search">` inside the `<search>` element. The input is exposed to assistive technology with the `searchbox` role, and the wrapper creates a landmark that screen reader users can jump to.

```html
<search>
  <form action="/search">
    <label for="q">Search articles</label>
    <input id="q" name="q" type="search" />
    <button type="submit">Search</button>
  </form>
</search>
```

If `<search>` is not an option, `role="search"` on the `<form>` gives the same landmark. A magnifying glass alone is not a label, so give the input a visible label or an `aria-label`, and name any icon-only [button](node:Button).

Some browsers show a clear icon, and Chrome also clears the field on Escape. Do not rely on either. If clearing matters, add your own labelled control and return focus to the input afterwards.

| Need                                | Use                                       |
| ----------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| Query that returns a results page   | Search field                              |
| Live filter of a visible list       | Search field with a status message        |
| Suggestions to choose from          | [Combobox](node:Combobox)                 |
| Jump to commands across the product | [Command palette](node:Command%20palette) |

Live results have two common failures. The first is silence: the list changes, but a screen reader user hears nothing. WCAG 4.1.3 treats text such as "5 results returned" as a status message, so put the count in a `role="status"` element that exists before the update.

The second is a race. Requests sent on each keystroke can return out of order, so results for "car" can overwrite results for "cart" while the field still reads "cart". Debounce input, which means waiting for a short pause in typing, and cancel or ignore stale requests with an `AbortController`.

Keep the query in the URL so results can be shared. When nothing matches, show an [empty state](node:Empty%20state) that repeats the query and suggests a next step.
quotes: Search sometimes shows results for what I typed two letters ago.
The search field has a response race. Abort the previous request on each new query.

nodes.name: Rich text editor
nodes.description: An editing surface for formatted content such as headings, lists and links, usually built on contenteditable.
nodes.markdown:
A rich text editor is an editing surface for formatted content such as headings, lists and links. It is usually built on the `contenteditable` attribute, which makes an element editable in the browser. Choose it only when people need formatting. A [textarea](node:Textarea), optionally with Markdown, is less work and has fewer failure modes.

| Option                       | Fits                                 | Cost                       |
| ---------------------------- | ------------------------------------ | -------------------------- |
| Plain textarea               | Comments, notes                      | No formatting              |
| Textarea with Markdown       | Technical audiences                  | Users learn syntax         |
| Editor library               | Documents, CMS content               | Bundle size, integration   |
| Custom on `contenteditable`  | Rarely justified                     | High maintenance           |

Browsers produce inconsistent markup from the same keystrokes, so mature editors keep their own document model and treat the DOM as a rendering of it. The older `document.execCommand` API is deprecated and implemented inconsistently, so new work should not depend on it. The `beforeinput` event is the usual place to intercept edits, though autocorrect and input method editors (used to compose languages such as Japanese) may skip it.

Pasted content needs cleaning. Content copied from a word processor can bring in pages of inline styles, and pasted or stored HTML can carry scripts. Sanitise on paste, and again on the server before displaying saved content, because client checks can be bypassed.

For assistive technology, give the editable region `role="textbox"`, `aria-multiline="true"` and an accessible name. Formatting commands belong in a labelled [toolbar](node:Toolbar) with a single Tab stop, and [buttons](node:Button) such as Bold should expose `aria-pressed`.

If Tab indents text, keyboard users can get stuck, which WCAG 2.1.2 prohibits unless they are told how to leave. Keep Tab for moving focus, or document a way out such as Escape then Tab. The Authoring Practices also recommend a documented shortcut from the text to the toolbar.

Pair the editor with [autosave](node:Autosave).
quotes: Pasting from Word turned the article into a wall of inline styles.
The rich text editor isn't sanitising paste. Strip it to our allowed elements.

nodes.name: Form field
nodes.description: The unit that groups a label, control, hint and error message so that they work together.
nodes.markdown: A form field is the unit that groups a label, a control, optional hint text and an error message. Design systems usually provide it as a wrapper so every input gets the same layout. The parts must be connected in the markup as well as placed near each other. | Part | Element | Connected with | | ------- | ----------------------- | ------------------------------------ | | Label | `
quotes: Clicking the Billing email label focuses the Shipping email input.
Both form fields use the same hard-coded `id`. Generate one per instance.

nodes.name: Helper text
nodes.description: Short persistent guidance attached to a form control that explains what to enter or how the value will be used.
nodes.markdown:
Helper text is short, persistent guidance attached to a form control. It explains what to enter, the expected format, or how the value will be used, such as "We only use this to send receipts". It sits beside the input in a [form field](node:Form%20field), and stays visible while the person types. Each place for guidance has limits. | Where guidance goes | When it works | Why it can fail | | ---------------------------------- | -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------- | | Label | Naming the field | Becomes long and slow to hear | | Helper text | Format rules, consequences | Ignored if it is too long | | Placeholder | A short optional example | Disappears on typing | | [Tooltip](node:Tooltip) | Optional extra detail | Hidden until requested, hard on touch | Connect the text to the control with `aria-describedby`, so a screen reader (software that reads the interface aloud) announces it after the label and role when the field receives focus. ```html

Use at least 12 characters.

``` A common failure is revealing a requirement only after the mistake. A password field gives no rules, the user submits, and only then learns the minimum length. State constraints before input. WCAG 3.3.2 requires labels or instructions where content requires user input. A related bug is replacing helper text with the error message. Once the field is invalid, the rule that would help the person fix it disappears. Keep the helper text and add the error next to it, or write the error so that it restates the rule. If both are shown, list both ids in `aria-describedby`. Text below a field can be covered by an on-screen keyboard or a popup, so format rules are often easier to see between the label and the input. Keep it to one short sentence, and reserve it for fields where people might otherwise get it wrong.
quotes: People only learn the password rules after the form rejects them.
Move the rules into helper text under the label, and keep them visible when the error appears.

nodes.name: Inline validation
nodes.description: Checking a form field and showing the result next to it before or at submission, rather than only after a full page reload.
nodes.markdown:
Inline validation is checking a field and showing the result next to it, instead of waiting until a submitted form comes back with errors. A common failure is an error that appears too soon: a person types the first letter of an email address and is immediately told it is invalid.

Timing decides whether it helps.

| When to check   | Suits                                    | Risk                               |
| --------------- | ---------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| On each input   | Password rules, character counts, fixing an existing error | Errors while still typing |
| When leaving the field | Format checks such as email or date | Focus moves before the user reads it |
| On submit       | Every field, always                      | Late feedback if used alone        |

A common pattern waits until the user leaves a field before first showing an error, then re-checks on each input while they fix it. The CSS `:user-invalid` selector supports this, because it matches only after the user has interacted with the control, whereas `:invalid` matches an empty required field on page load.

```css
input:user-invalid {
  border-color: var(--danger);
}
```

Also validate on submit and on the server.

WCAG 3.3.1 requires that errors are identified and described in text, so a red border is not enough. Put the message in the [form field](node:Form%20field), link it with `aria-describedby`, and set `aria-invalid="true"` only after the value has failed. The W3C forms tutorial suggests `aria-live="polite"` for feedback while typing, so that the message is read when the user pauses instead of on every keystroke.

Say what to do, such as "Enter a date in the format DD/MM/YYYY", rather than "Invalid input". Keep the submit [button](node:Button) enabled so people can submit and see an [error summary](node:Error%20summary).

Async checks, such as username availability, need a pending state and must ignore stale responses.
quotes: The email field turns red as soon as I type one letter.
The inline validation runs on input. Wait for blur first, then re-check while they fix it.

nodes.name: Error summary
nodes.description: A list of form errors shown after submission, with each item linking to the field that needs fixing.
nodes.markdown:
An error summary is a list of everything wrong with a submitted form, shown at the top, where each item links to the field that needs fixing. On a long form, it addresses a specific problem: the user presses Submit, nothing appears to change, and the error is out of view further up the page. It works alongside [inline validation](node:Inline%20validation) rather than replacing it. The summary gives the overview and a route to each problem, and the message beside each [form field](node:Form%20field) explains the fix in context. ```html

There are 2 problems with your application

  • Enter an email address
  • Date of birth must be in the past
``` | Step | What happens | | ---- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- | | 1 | User submits. Validation finds errors | | 2 | Summary renders above the form, and entered values are preserved | | 3 | Focus moves to the summary, or to the first invalid field | | 4 | User follows a link, and focus lands in that input | | 5 | User fixes it, and the summary updates on the next submit | The W3C forms tutorial recommends a list before the form, under a distinctive heading, with each item naming the problem and linking to the control. It advises moving focus to the first invalid field, while WCAG technique G139 shows focus moving to the error list. Pick one approach and apply it across the product. Several failures are common. Links that point to a wrapper rather than the input scroll the page but leave focus behind, so use the control's `id`. A [sticky header](node:Sticky%20header) can cover the target after the jump, which `scroll-padding-block-start` prevents. Clearing the user's entries on error forces them to start again, and technique G139 explicitly says to keep them. For server-rendered forms, also prefix the page `` with "Error:" so that screen reader users hear the outcome as the page loads. If script inserts the summary without moving focus, `role="alert"` announces it.
quotes: Users hit Submit and think the form is broken.
The error is off-screen. Add an error summary at the top and move focus to it.

nodes.name: Input mask
nodes.description: Formatting applied to an input as the user types, such as adding spaces to a card number or brackets to a phone number.
nodes.markdown:
An input mask is formatting applied to a [text field](node:Text%20field) as the user types, such as grouping a card number into fours or adding brackets to a phone number. It rewrites the field's value while someone is typing into it, which is where most of its bugs come from.

A common symptom is a caret that jumps. The user goes back to fix a digit in the middle, the script reformats the value, and the caret lands at the end, so the next keystroke goes in the wrong place. Other failures follow the same cause: pasted values are rejected or doubled, browser autofill is garbled, and deletion stops at a separator that the mask immediately puts back.

Choose the lightest option that solves the problem.

| Approach                | How it works                              | Risk   |
| ----------------------- | ----------------------------------------- | ------ |
| Helper hint only        | Shows the format, accepts anything        | Lowest |
| Normalise on the server | Strips spaces and punctuation             | Low    |
| Format on blur          | Reformats when focus leaves               | Low    |
| Format while typing     | Rewrites on each input                    | High   |
| Fixed-slot mask         | Shows `__/__/____` and blocks other keys  | Highest |

Often it is enough to accept any reasonable format and clean it up afterwards.

If you format while typing, keep the raw value separate from the display value, restore the caret after each change, and handle paste. Do not depend on `beforeinput` alone, because autofill, spellcheck and input method editors (used to compose languages such as Japanese) may skip it. Use the `input` event as the final check.

A screen reader may read placeholder underscores aloud or announce each inserted character, so test with one. Keep `autocomplete` tokens such as `cc-number`, put the format in [helper text](node:Helper%20text), and avoid fixed masks for international phone numbers and postcodes, which vary in length and grouping.
quotes: When I fix a digit in the card number, the cursor jumps to the end.
The input mask rewrites the value on every keystroke. Format on blur instead.

nodes.name: Multi-step form
nodes.description: A long form split into a sequence of screens, with progress shown and answers kept between steps.
nodes.markdown:
A multi-step form is a long form split into a sequence of screens, such as Address, Delivery, Payment and Review. Use it when the questions fall into clear groups, or when later questions depend on earlier answers. A short form is easier on one page.

The main risk is lost work. Someone reaches step four, presses the browser's Back control to check an answer, and the form returns to an empty first step. Give each step its own URL, and save answers as the user leaves each one.

| Stage        | What the interface does                                        |
| ------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Start        | States how many steps there are                                |
| Each step    | Shows position in the title and heading, for example "Step 2 of 4" |
| Next         | Validates this step and saves its answers                      |
| Back         | Returns with answers intact, and does not validate             |
| Review       | Shows all answers, with a link to change each                  |
| Submit       | Sends the data and confirms the result                         |

Show progress with a [stepper](node:Stepper) for a fixed sequence. If the number of steps depends on answers, the W3C forms tutorial suggests the `<progress>` element instead. Mark the current item with `aria-current="step"`.

When a step changes without a page load, move focus to the new step's heading (with `tabindex="-1"`) and update the document title, or screen reader users get no sign that anything changed.

Two WCAG criteria apply. Redundant Entry (3.3.7) says information already provided in the same process must be filled in or offered for selection, with narrow exceptions, so offer "same as delivery address" for billing. Error Prevention (3.3.4) requires legal, financial and data-changing submissions to be reversible, checked or confirmed, and a review step provides confirmation.

Validate each step on Next using [inline validation](node:Inline%20validation) and an [error summary](node:Error%20summary).
quotes: People press back on the payment step and lose their whole address.
The multi-step form keeps answers in component state. Put each step in the URL and persist the draft.

nodes.name: Autosave
nodes.description: Saving a user's work automatically as they edit, so that it survives a closed tab or failed connection.
nodes.markdown:
Autosave is saving a user's work automatically as they edit, without a Save [button](node:Button). It protects against losing a draft when a tab closes, a laptop dies or a connection drops. It suits documents, notes and settings. It does not suit actions with consequences, such as publishing or paying, where a change should stay a draft until the person commits to it.

| Step    | Who     | What happens                                    |
| ------- | ------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| Edit    | User    | Changes content. Status becomes "Unsaved"       |
| Wait    | Client  | Debounce, which waits for a pause in typing     |
| Send    | Client  | Sends changes with a version number. "Saving"   |
| Confirm | Server  | Stores them. Status becomes "Saved"             |
| Fail    | Client  | Keeps changes locally, retries and tells the user |

A false "Saved" label causes data loss. If the status updates before the server responds, or a failed request goes unnoticed, the person closes the tab believing their work is safe. Show the status from the actual result, and make failure visible.

Requests can also finish out of order, so an older save can overwrite a newer one. Send one save at a time per document, or attach a version so the server rejects stale writes. The same check detects edits from a second tab or device, so decide how to resolve that conflict.

For leaving the page, MDN recommends saving on `visibilitychange`, since `beforeunload` and `unload` often do not fire on mobile. Use `fetch` with `keepalive` or `navigator.sendBeacon` for the final small payload. A `beforeunload` handler, added only while work is unsaved, can show the browser's generic warning.

Expose the status with `role="status"` (WCAG 4.1.3), but announce failures and recovery rather than every save, or a screen reader user hears "Saved" throughout their writing. Provide version history or an [undo pattern](node:Undo%20pattern) for changes people regret.
quotes: It said Saved, but my last paragraph is gone after the refresh.
Autosave sets the label before the request finishes. Update it only when the server confirms.

nodes.name: Navbar
nodes.description: A horizontal bar of primary site links, usually at the top of every page, often collapsing into a menu on small screens.
nodes.markdown:
A navbar is a horizontal bar of primary links, usually at the top of every page, holding the logo, main sections and account controls. It suits products with a small number of top-level destinations. When there are many sections or deep hierarchy, a [sidebar](node:Sidebar) has more room. On phones, [bottom navigation](node:Bottom%20navigation) puts the same destinations within reach of the thumb. Build it from a `
` containing a list of links, and mark the current page. ```html
  • Home
  • Pricing
``` If a page has several `
` elements, give each a unique label. Leave out the word "navigation", because the role is announced as well, and "Main navigation navigation" is what the user would hear. Keep links in the same relative order across pages, which WCAG 3.2.3 requires. A common accessibility mistake is applying ARIA menu roles to site links. `role="menu"` promises desktop-application behaviour, including arrow-key movement, and removes the list semantics people expect. The WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices say the disclosure pattern is better suited to most websites. | Part | Build it as | Keyboard | | ---------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------- | | Link | `` | Tab, Enter | | Section dropdown | [`
quotes: When I tab back up the page, focused links disappear under the header.
The navbar is sticky. Add `scroll-padding-block-start` matching its height.

nodes.name: Sidebar
nodes.description: A vertical panel beside the main content, usually holding navigation or filters, that can often collapse.
nodes.markdown:
A sidebar is a vertical panel beside the main content, usually holding navigation, filters or supporting information. It suits applications with many sections, because a vertical list has room to grow and can show nested groups. For a handful of destinations, a [navbar](node:Navbar) uses less space. A sidebar stays on screen alongside the content, whereas a [drawer](node:Drawer) opens over it on demand.

The right element depends on what it contains.

| Content                        | Element                                     |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------- |
| Links to other pages           | `<nav aria-label="Project">`                |
| Related supporting content     | `<aside>`                                   |
| Filters for the current list   | A labelled form or group within the page    |

Sidebars often have three display states.

| State     | Display                  | Requirement                                     |
| --------- | ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------- |
| Expanded  | Icons and labels         | Mark the current link with `aria-current="page"` |
| Rail      | Icons only               | Every link keeps an accessible name             |
| Hidden    | Nothing                  | Contents leave the Tab order                    |

A common bug affects the hidden state. A sidebar moved off-screen with `transform` is invisible, but its links remain focusable, so a keyboard user tabs through a dozen stops with no visible [focus ring](node:Focus%20ring). Set `hidden` or `inert` on it when closed. If you animate the exit, apply it once the transition ends.

The collapse control should be a real [button](node:Button) with `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls`, with a name that matches its purpose, such as "Project navigation". In a collapsed rail, add a [tooltip](node:Tooltip) so sighted users can learn each icon, and show it on focus as well as hover.

On small screens a fixed sidebar takes most of the viewport, and WCAG 1.4.10 expects content to reflow at a width of 320 CSS pixels. Below a set [breakpoint](node:Breakpoint), turn it into a drawer. If the hierarchy runs several levels deep, nested disclosure lists or a [tree view](node:Tree%20view) can structure it.
quotes: Tab seems to vanish for about ten presses after the header.
It's going through the collapsed sidebar off-screen. Set `inert` on it when it's closed.

nodes.name: Breadcrumb
nodes.description: A trail of links showing the current page's parent pages in the site hierarchy.
nodes.markdown:
A breadcrumb is a trail of links showing where the current page sits in a site's hierarchy, such as Home, Shoes, Running, Trail Pro. It lets people move up a level without using search or the main menu. It suits sites with deep structures, such as stores and documentation. On a flat site with two levels it adds clutter. A breadcrumb shows hierarchy, while browser history records visits. The common design mistake is mixing them by building the trail from the pages a person happened to visit. The trail then differs for each visitor and stops telling them where the page belongs. The WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices define a simple structure: a labelled navigation landmark containing an ordered list of links. ```html
  1. Home
  2. Shoes
  3. Trail Pro
``` | Part | Requirement | | ----------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- | | Container | `
` with `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby` | | List | `
    `, because order carries meaning | | Current item | `aria-current="page"` if it is a link, optional if plain text | | Separators | Added in CSS so they are not read aloud | No special keyboard behaviour is required. The links are ordinary Tab stops, and the pattern lists keyboard interaction as not applicable. Do not add arrow-key handling or menu roles. Separators typed into the markup may be read aloud by a screen reader (software that reads the interface aloud). Draw them with a `::before` pseudo-element instead. Long trails can overflow on small screens. Common fixes are letting the list wrap, showing only the parent as a "Back to Shoes" link, or collapsing the middle levels behind a [button](node:Button) with an ellipsis. That button needs a name such as "Show full path", and hidden levels must remain reachable. Truncating with CSS alone cuts off the page names people use to orient themselves.
quotes: Why does the breadcrumb change depending on how I got to this product?
It's built from browsing history. It should come from the category tree.

nodes.name: Tabs
nodes.description: A row of labels that switches between panels of related content in the same place, showing one panel at a time.
nodes.markdown:
Tabs are a row of labels that switch between panels of related content in the same place, showing one panel at a time. A settings screen with Profile, Billing and Team sections is a typical use. Choose them when people work with one section at a time and do not need to compare them. If they might need several sections open together, use an [accordion](node:Accordion). If each label goes to a separate page, use links in a [navbar](node:Navbar) with `aria-current="page"`, because tab roles there misdescribe what happens. ```html
...
...
``` The tab list is one Tab stop, and arrow keys move within it. | Key | Action | | ----------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- | | Tab | Enters at the active tab, then moves on to the panel | | Left, Right Arrow | Previous or next tab, wrapping at the ends | | Home, End | Optionally first or last tab | | Enter, Space | Activates the tab, if it does not activate on focus | In a vertical tab list, set `aria-orientation="vertical"` and use Up and Down Arrow instead. Activation can be automatic, where arrowing to a tab shows its panel, or manual, where the user presses Enter or Space. The Authoring Practices recommend automatic activation only when panels appear without noticeable delay. If each panel fetches data, automatic activation fires a request for every tab the user passes through, so use manual. A panel with no focusable content, or whose first element is not focusable, should have `tabindex="0"` so that keyboard users can reach it. Two state bugs are common. Unmounting a hidden panel discards anything typed in it, so a half-completed form is empty when the user comes back. Keep panels mounted and use `hidden`. And if the active tab lives only in memory, refreshing or sharing the link resets it, so reflect it in the URL.
quotes: I filled in Billing, checked Profile, and my Billing draft is gone.
The tabs unmount inactive panels. Keep them mounted and toggle `hidden`.

nodes.name: Pagination control
nodes.description: A set of links for moving through a long result set one page at a time, with previous, next and numbered pages.
nodes.markdown:
A pagination control is a set of links for moving through a long result set one page at a time, usually with Previous, Next and numbered pages. It gives people a stable position they can return to, share and reason about, such as "page 4". That suits search results, admin lists and a [data table](node:Data%20table). [Infinite scroll](node:Infinite%20scroll) suits casual browsing feeds, but it makes the footer hard to reach and a position hard to keep. A "Load more" [button](node:Button) sits between the two. Build it as a labelled `
` containing real links, so that each page has a URL. ```html
  • Previous
  • 2
  • 3
  • 4
  • Next
``` | Part | Detail | | ---------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- | | Current | `aria-current="page"` plus a non-colour visual cue | | Numbers | Named "Page 3", since a bare "3" is unclear out of context | | Previous | On page 1, remove it or disable it | | Ellipsis | Plain text, hidden from assistive technology | Keep the visible number inside any accessible name, as WCAG 2.5.3 (Label in Name) requires, so that voice-control users can say what they see. No custom keyboard handling is needed. Links are ordinary Tab stops. When results load without a full page navigation, two problems appear. Focus stays on a link that may have been re-rendered or removed, and nothing tells a screen reader user that the list changed. Move focus to the results heading, or announce "Page 3 of 12" in a `role="status"` region, and scroll to the top of the list. Numbered pages built on a database offset can drift. If rows are inserted while someone is reading, items shift across the page boundary, so one record appears twice or another is skipped. For fast-changing data, cursor pagination, which asks for rows after the last one seen, keeps the sequence stable, at the cost of jumping directly to page 37.
quotes: The same order shows up on page 2 and page 3.
New rows are shifting the offset. Switch that pagination control to a cursor.

nodes.name: Stepper
nodes.description: A progress indicator showing the steps of a process, which are complete and which one the user is on.
nodes.markdown:
A stepper is a progress indicator showing the stages of a process, which ones are complete and which one the user is on. It usually sits at the top of a [multi-step form](node:Multi-step%20form), such as Address, Delivery, Payment, Review.
