The word is also used for the plus and minus [buttons](node:Button) on a [number input](node:Number%20input), which is a different control. | Component | Shows | | --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ | | Stepper | Named stages and the current one | | [Progress bar](node:Progress%20bar) | How much is done, with no stage names | | [Tabs](node:Tabs) | Sections in any order | | [Breadcrumb](node:Breadcrumb) | Position in a site hierarchy | Use a stepper when the sequence is known and short enough to show. If the number of steps depends on earlier answers, a fixed list will mislead people, so a progress bar or "Step 2" without a total is more honest. Build it as an ordered list, and mark the current step. ```html
  1. Completed: Address
  2. Delivery
  3. Payment
``` `aria-current="step"` marks the active item. For finished steps, the W3C forms tutorial uses visually hidden text such as "Completed:". Colour alone fails WCAG 1.4.1, so change the shape too. Completed steps should be links, so people can go back and review their answers. Future steps should normally be plain text. A common failure is drawing every step as clickable: someone jumps to Payment before entering an address, and the form breaks or submits incomplete data. If the steps can be done in any order, a checklist or tabs describes that better. The stepper is not itself a keyboard widget. Links take normal Tab stops, and plain text items take none. When the step changes, move focus to the new heading, because updating the indicator alone is easy to miss. Horizontal steppers overflow on narrow screens. Stack them vertically, or show "Step 2 of 4: Delivery" as text.
quotes: Someone got to Payment without an address and the order failed.
Future steps in the stepper are clickable. Only link the steps they've completed.

nodes.name: Dropdown menu
nodes.description: A list of actions that opens from a button and closes after one is chosen.
nodes.markdown:
A dropdown menu is a list of actions that opens from a [button](node:Button) and usually closes after one is chosen, such as Rename, Duplicate and Delete under a "More" control. It holds actions. If the control sets a value in a form, use a [select](node:Select). If it holds links to site sections, use a disclosure: a button with `aria-expanded` that reveals an ordinary list of links. Mixing these up causes bugs. Adding `role="menu"` to site navigation tells screen readers to expect application-style keys, so people press arrows and nothing happens, or Tab closes the list before they reach the links. The WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices say a disclosure is better suited to most site navigation. ```html
  • Rename
  • Delete
``` | Key | Action | | ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ | | Enter, Space | On the button, opens and focuses the first item | | Down Arrow | On the button, optionally opens. In the menu, next item | | Up Arrow | In the menu, previous item | | Home, End | First or last item, if arrows do not wrap | | A letter | Optionally jumps to the next matching item | | Enter | Activates the item and closes the menu | | Escape | Closes and returns focus to the button | | Tab | Leaves the menu and closes it | Items can be `menuitem`, `menuitemcheckbox` or `menuitemradio`. Disabled items stay focusable so that people can discover them. Menus inside a scrolling container or table are often clipped by `overflow: hidden`. Rendering through a [portal](node:Portal), or using the [popover](node:Popover) attribute with [anchor positioning](node:Anchor%20positioning), lifts the menu above the page. After an item runs, focus needs a destination. If "Delete" removes the row containing the button, focus falls to the page body and the user loses their place. Send it to the next row or a nearby heading.
quotes: The row actions menu gets cut off by the table.
The table has `overflow: auto`. Render the dropdown menu in the top layer with the Popover API.

nodes.name: Context menu
nodes.description: A menu of actions for the item under the pointer, opened by right-click, long press or a keyboard command.
quotes: I can't right-click a link to open it in a new tab anymore.
Our context menu handler is on `document`. Scope it to the file rows.

nodes.name: Command palette
nodes.description: A keyboard-opened search box that finds and runs commands or jumps to pages from anywhere in an application.
nodes.markdown:
A command palette is a search box, opened with a keyboard shortcut, that finds and runs commands or jumps to pages from anywhere in an application. The person presses a shortcut, types a few letters of "invite user", and presses Enter. It suits large products used often by experienced people, and every command must also exist somewhere visible.

Compared with a [search field](node:Search%20field), which returns content, a palette mainly returns actions. Compared with a [dropdown menu](node:Dropdown%20menu), it scales to hundreds of items because people filter them by typing.

It is usually composed from existing patterns: a [modal dialog](node:Modal%20dialog) containing a [combobox](node:Combobox) with a listbox of results.

| Key             | Action                                      |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| Ctrl or Cmd + K | Opens the palette (a common convention)     |
| Typing          | Filters results                             |
| Up, Down Arrow  | Moves the highlighted result                |
| Enter           | Runs the highlighted command                |
| Escape          | Closes and returns focus to where it was    |

DOM focus stays in the input while `aria-activedescendant` identifies the highlighted option, so typing keeps working. Announce the count with a `role="status"` message such as "6 results", because WCAG 4.1.3 covers this kind of update.

Keyboard shortcuts can conflict with browsers and with typing. Some browsers use Ctrl+K for their own search or address bar. A single-character shortcut such as `/` fires while someone types in a field unless you check the event target, and WCAG 2.1.4 requires that such shortcuts can be turned off or remapped, or work only while the relevant component has focus. Provide a visible [button](node:Button) that opens the palette.

After a command runs, send focus to its result, such as the page it opened. If the command acts on the current view, return focus to the element that had it before.
quotes: Typing a slash in the comment box keeps opening the command palette.
The shortcut listener doesn't check for inputs. Ignore it when focus is in an editable field.

nodes.name: Bottom navigation
nodes.description: A fixed bar along the bottom of a mobile screen with links to a small number of top-level destinations.
nodes.markdown:
Bottom navigation is a fixed bar along the bottom of a mobile screen, with links to a small number of top-level destinations, commonly three to five. Each item pairs an icon with a short label. It keeps the main sections within reach of the thumb and visible at all times. With more destinations than fit, use a [drawer](node:Drawer) or a "More" item. On wide screens, a [sidebar](node:Sidebar) or [navbar](node:Navbar) usually replaces it. Although it can look like a row of [tabs](node:Tabs), it navigates between destinations, so it should be a `
` containing links rather than an ARIA tab list. ```html
Home Orders
``` ```css .bottom-nav { position: fixed; inset-inline: 0; bottom: 0; padding-block-end: env(safe-area-inset-bottom); } ``` Each link is a normal Tab stop, activated with Enter. Screen readers announce the visible text and `aria-current="page"` for the current destination. Keep the labels visible, because icons alone are ambiguous. | Symptom | Cause | Fix | | -------------------------------------- | ------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | | Last list item hidden behind the bar | Fixed bar overlaps content | Add bottom padding to the main region | | Bar sits under the home indicator | Ignores the [safe area](node:Safe%20area) | Pad with the `env()` inset | | Focused link hidden while tabbing | Bar covers it (WCAG 2.4.11) | Set `scroll-padding-block-end` | | Bar floats above the on-screen keyboard | Viewport resizes on input | Hide it while a [text field](node:Text%20field) has focus | | Mis-taps on neighbouring items | Small targets | Size each item as a generous [touch target](node:Touch%20target) | State preservation is the less visible problem. If tapping a section resets its scroll position and filters, people lose their place every time they compare two sections. Keep each section's state when moving away. Tapping the current item again conventionally scrolls that section to the top. Mark the current item with more than colour, as WCAG 1.4.1 requires. A filled icon, an indicator or a bolder label works.
quotes: Checkout is stuck behind the tab bar on iPhones.
The bottom navigation overlaps the page. Pad the content by its height plus the safe-area inset.

nodes.name: Tree view
nodes.description: A hierarchical list whose parent items expand and collapse, navigated with arrow keys, such as a file explorer.
nodes.markdown:
A tree view is a hierarchical list whose parent items expand and collapse, such as the file explorer in a code editor. It suits deep, browsable structures where people move around and act on items. Do not use it for ordinary site navigation. A nested list of links with disclosure [buttons](node:Button) is simpler and is what most sites need, because ARIA tree roles replace normal link and Tab behaviour with application-style keys. The whole tree takes one Tab stop, usually managed with a [roving tabindex](node:Roving%20tabindex). | Key | Action | | --------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- | | Up, Down Arrow | Previous or next visible node | | Right Arrow | Opens a closed node, or moves to the first child of an open one | | Left Arrow | Closes an open node, or moves to the parent | | Home, End | First or last visible node | | Enter | Performs the node's default action | | Letter keys | Type-ahead to a matching node | | `*` | Optionally expands all siblings at that level | ```html
  • src
    • index.ts
``` Only parent nodes get `aria-expanded`. Putting `aria-expanded="false"` on a leaf is a common bug, because a screen reader then announces a file as collapsed, and the user tries to open something that has no children. Moving focus and selecting are separate. In a [multi-select](node:Multi-select) tree, the recommended model uses Space to toggle the focused node, so arrow keys can move without clearing the existing selection. Large trees are often loaded on demand or rendered as a [virtualized list](node:Virtualized%20list). When not all nodes are in the DOM, `aria-level`, `aria-setsize` and `aria-posinset` are required, or screen readers report wrong positions. Make the arrow a distinct target for expanding and the label a target for activating. When a parent collapses around the focused child, move focus to the parent.
quotes: VoiceOver says every file in the project is collapsed.
The tree view sets `aria-expanded` on leaf nodes too. Only parents should have it.

nodes.name: Skip link
nodes.description: A link at the start of a page that lets keyboard users jump past repeated navigation to the main content.
nodes.markdown:
A skip link is a link at the start of a page that lets keyboard users jump past repeated navigation to the main content. Without one, someone using only the keyboard must Tab through every item in the [navbar](node:Navbar) and [sidebar](node:Sidebar) on each page before reaching what they came for. It is usually hidden until it receives focus, so most mouse users never see it. ```html Skip to main content
...
...
``` ```css .skip-link { position: absolute; transform: translateY(-200%); } .skip-link:focus { transform: none; } ``` It should be the first focusable element. Pressing Tab on page load reveals it, Enter activates it, and the next Tab continues from inside `
`. `tabindex="-1"` on the target lets it take focus programmatically without adding a Tab stop. WCAG 2.4.1, Bypass Blocks (Level A), requires a way to skip content repeated across pages. Skip links are one sufficient technique. Headings and landmarks, such as `
` and `
`, are also listed, and screen reader users often navigate by them. Those shortcuts are not available to sighted keyboard users without extra tools, so a skip link remains useful alongside them. | Failure | Cause | Fix | | ------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- | | Link never appears | Hidden with `display: none` | Move it off-screen or clip it | | Visible but under the header | Lower stacking than a sticky bar | Raise its `z-index` | | Nothing happens on Enter | Target `id` is missing | Add the `id` to `
` | | Router intercepts the link | `#main` treated as a route change | Handle it and focus the target | | Target hidden after the jump | [Sticky header](node:Sticky%20header) covers it | Set `scroll-padding-block-start` | In single-page applications, the route changes without a page load and focus may stay in the previous view. After navigation, move focus to the new page's heading or the top of the document. When revealed, the link needs a clear [focus ring](node:Focus%20ring).
quotes: I have to tab through forty nav links on every page.
We need a skip link as the first focusable element, pointing at `main`.

nodes.name: Modal dialog
nodes.description: A window over the page that blocks everything behind it until the user completes or dismisses it.
nodes.markdown:
A modal dialog is a window over the page that blocks everything behind it until the user completes or dismisses it. Use it for a short, focused task that must be finished or abandoned before continuing, such as editing a record. If people need to refer to the page while working, use a non-modal [drawer](node:Drawer) or a [popover](node:Popover). For a confirmation that demands a decision, use an [alert dialog](node:Alert%20dialog). Use the native `` element and open it with `showModal()`. ```html

Edit address

 ``` | Behaviour | `showModal()` provides | You still do | | --------------------------- | ---------------------- | ------------------------------- | | Renders above all content | Yes, in the top layer | Style the `::backdrop` | | Makes the page inert | Yes | Nothing | | Moves focus inside | Yes | Use `autofocus` where it helps | | Closes on Escape | Yes | Handle `cancel` to guard drafts | | Returns focus on close | Yes | Handle a removed trigger | | Names the dialog | No | Add `aria-labelledby` | | Stops the page scrolling | No | Add a [scroll lock](node:Scroll%20lock) | Content behind the dialog cannot receive focus. A custom build has to reproduce this with a [focus trap](node:Focus%20trap). Do not put `tabindex` on the `` element, which the HTML specification forbids. Initial focus depends on the content. The first control is the default. For long content, focus a heading with `tabindex="-1"` so the top is not scrolled out of view. Always include a visible close control, because not everyone has an Escape key. Closing on an outside click is risky for forms because a stray click discards work. The `closedby` attribute controls this, but MDN lists it as limited availability. If the trigger is gone when the dialog closes, such as after deleting its row, move focus to a logical nearby element yourself. Otherwise focus falls to the page body and keyboard users lose their place.
quotes: Keyboard users can tab to the page behind our edit popup.
It's a styled `div`. Make it a real modal dialog with `showModal()`.

nodes.name: Alert dialog
nodes.description: A modal dialog that interrupts the user with an important message and requires a response, such as confirming a deletion.
nodes.markdown:
An alert dialog is a [modal dialog](node:Modal%20dialog) that interrupts the user with an important message and requires a response, such as "Delete this project?". The `alertdialog` role tells assistive technology that this is an urgent interruption, and some platforms treat it specially, for example by playing a system sound. Use it only when the person must decide before continuing. | Situation | Use | | --------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- | | Irreversible, serious action | Alert dialog | | Reversible action | Do it, then offer an [undo pattern](node:Undo%20pattern) | | Result of a completed action | [Toast](node:Toast) | | Problem tied to part of the page | [Inline alert](node:Inline%20alert) | Overuse is the common failure. When every action asks "Are you sure?", people learn to press the confirm [button](node:Button) without reading, so the one that matters gets the same reflex. Reserve the pattern for actions that cannot be undone, and offer undo for the rest. ```html

Delete project?

This removes 12 environments and cannot be undone.

 ``` Open it with `showModal()` to get the same inert background, focus handling and Escape behaviour as any modal. The title is linked with `aria-labelledby`, and the message with `aria-describedby`, so that a screen reader announces both as the dialog opens. For destructive actions, the WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices advise that initial focus may go to the least destructive control. If the focus lands on Delete, an accidental Enter or Space, perhaps from a key held down from the previous step, causes the loss the dialog was meant to prevent. Escape should act as Cancel, and clicking the backdrop should not count as confirmation. Button labels should state the outcome. "Delete project" and "Keep project" can be understood without reading the message, while "OK" and "Cancel" are ambiguous for a question such as "Cancel this subscription?". When the dialog closes, focus returns to the trigger, or moves to a sensible neighbour if the trigger was deleted.
quotes: Someone double-pressed Enter and wiped their workspace.
The alert dialog focuses Delete on open. Autofocus Cancel instead.

nodes.name: Drawer
nodes.description: A panel that slides in from a screen edge to show navigation, details or a form, either modally or beside the page.
nodes.markdown:
A drawer is a panel that slides in from a screen edge to show navigation, details or a form. It keeps people on the current page and gives more room than a small dialog, which suits viewing a record from a list or holding filters. A [sidebar](node:Sidebar) is part of the page layout and stays open. A [modal dialog](node:Modal%20dialog) is centred and suits a short task. On phones, a [bottom sheet](node:Bottom%20sheet) is often the better form.

The first decision is whether it blocks the page.

| Type      | Page behind       | Focus                                   | Build with                  |
| --------- | ----------------- | --------------------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| Modal     | Inert, dimmed     | Moves in and stays in                   | `<dialog>` with `showModal()` |
| Non-modal | Still usable      | Follows the trigger in the Tab order    | `<aside>` or `show()`       |

A modal drawer is a dialog with different CSS. Using `<dialog>` provides the inert background, Escape handling and focus return.

```css
dialog.drawer {
  margin: 0 0 0 auto;
  height: 100dvh;
  max-height: none;
}
```

A non-modal drawer must sit next to its trigger in the DOM, or use an equivalent focus order. WCAG 2.4.3 requires a focus order that preserves meaning, and a panel at the end of the document forces keyboard users to Tab through the entire page to reach what they just opened. Keep a labelled close [button](node:Button), and let Escape close it while focus is inside.

A closed drawer can remain in the Tab order. Moved off-screen with `transform`, it stays focusable, so Tab disappears into invisible links and screen readers read content nobody can see. A closed `<dialog>` avoids this. For a custom panel, apply `inert` or `hidden` when closed, after any exit animation ends.

Slide animations should respect [reduced motion](node:Reduced%20motion). A modal drawer also needs a [scroll lock](node:Scroll%20lock) so the page behind does not move.
quotes: With the filter panel closed, Tab still lands on invisible controls.
The drawer is only translated off-screen. Set `inert` when it's closed.

nodes.name: Bottom sheet
nodes.description: A panel that rises from the bottom of a mobile screen, often draggable between heights, for options or supporting content.
quotes: Scrolling up in the filters keeps closing the whole sheet.
The bottom sheet drag is firing during scroll. Only start it when the list is at the top.

nodes.name: Popover
nodes.description: A non-modal floating panel opened from a control, showing content above the page while the rest stays usable.
nodes.markdown:
A popover is a non-modal floating panel opened from a control, such as a date filter or a small settings panel. The rest of the page stays usable, and it usually closes on an outside click. Choose it for short supplementary content that may contain controls. Use a [tooltip](node:Tooltip) for a brief text hint, and a [modal dialog](node:Modal%20dialog) when the page must be blocked. The HTML Popover API handles the mechanics declaratively. ```html
...
``` | Value | Closes on outside click or Escape | Other popovers | | -------- | --------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- | | `auto` | Yes | Closes unrelated `auto` popovers | | `hint` | Yes | Leaves `auto` popovers open | | `manual` | No | Independent, several can be open | A bare `popover` attribute means `auto`. MDN lists the API as widely available since April 2024, with some parts varying, so check `hint` support. An open popover is placed in the browser's top layer, above the page regardless of `z-index`. This avoids clipping by a parent with `overflow: hidden` and the stacking problems that previously required a [portal](node:Portal). Keyboard behaviour differs from a dialog. Opening a popover does not move focus into it. The browser places it next in the Tab order after its invoker, so the next Tab enters it. Closing with Escape returns focus to the invoker. If the content should receive focus at once, add `autofocus` to an element inside. The attribute adds no semantic role, so a plain `
` is announced as nothing in particular. Add a suitable role, such as `dialog` with a label for a panel of controls, or use a list of links. A `popovertarget` [button](node:Button) gets an implicit expanded state, so do not manage `aria-expanded` by hand. By default an open popover is centred in the viewport, so pair it with [anchor positioning](node:Anchor%20positioning).
quotes: The filter panel gets clipped by the table's scroll container.
Make it a popover. It renders in the top layer, so `overflow` can't cut it off.

nodes.name: Tooltip
nodes.description: A small text label that appears on hover or keyboard focus to describe a control, and contains nothing interactive.
nodes.markdown:
A tooltip is a small text label that appears when a control is hovered or receives keyboard focus, usually after a short delay. It describes that control, such as naming an [icon button](node:Icon%20button). It holds plain text only. If the content includes a link or [button](node:Button), use a [popover](node:Popover) or [hover card](node:Hover%20card), because focus never moves into a tooltip and a pointer user may not be able to reach it. The WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices tooltip pattern is marked as work in progress. It describes the following behaviour. ```html
Visible to everyone in the workspace
``` | Trigger | Behaviour | | --------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- | | Focus | Opens. Focus stays on the control | | Blur | Closes | | Pointer enter | Opens after a short delay | | Pointer leave | Closes, unless the pointer moved onto the tooltip | | Escape | Closes, with focus staying where it is | WCAG 1.4.13, Content on Hover or Focus, sets three requirements. The tooltip must be dismissible without moving the pointer or focus, which is why Escape matters. It must be hoverable, so someone using screen magnification can move onto it and read it. It must persist until the user leaves or dismisses it, so a timer that hides it fails. Essential information in a tooltip is out of reach for touch users, who have no hover. A tooltip on a disabled control may never appear, because a natively [disabled](node:Disabled%20state) button cannot receive focus and some browsers do not fire pointer events on it. Use `aria-disabled` or explain the reason in visible text. The `title` attribute is not a substitute either, since it is generally unavailable from the keyboard and on touch screens. Use `aria-describedby` when it adds a description. If it is the control's only name, use `aria-labelledby` instead. Placement is often handled with `popover="hint"` plus [anchor positioning](node:Anchor%20positioning), where supported.
quotes: The tooltip disappears when I try to move my mouse onto it to read it.
That fails WCAG 1.4.13. Keep it open while the pointer is over the tooltip itself.

nodes.name: Hover card
nodes.description: A rich preview that appears when hovering or focusing a link, such as a user's profile summary.
nodes.markdown:
A hover card is a rich preview that appears when someone hovers over or focuses a link, such as a profile summary on a username or a page preview on a wiki link. Because it depends on a pointer or focus, treat it as a convenience: everything inside must also be available at the link's destination.

| Component                  | Content               | Opens on        | Interactive |
| -------------------------- | --------------------- | --------------- | ----------- |
| [Tooltip](node:Tooltip)    | Short text            | Hover, focus    | No          |
| Hover card                 | Rich preview          | Hover, focus    | Sometimes   |
| [Popover](node:Popover)    | Panel of content      | Click           | Yes         |

The Authoring Practices tooltip pattern says hover content with focusable elements should be a non-modal dialog rather than a tooltip. A card with a "Follow" [button](node:Button) therefore needs a dialog role, a label, and a keyboard route into it. If that is too much, keep the card read-only and put the action on the destination page.

WCAG 1.4.13, Content on Hover or Focus, applies directly. The card must be dismissible with a key such as Escape without moving the pointer, stay open while the pointer is over it, and remain until the user moves away.

A hover card can close before the pointer reaches it. As the pointer crosses the gap between link and card, the link fires `mouseleave` and the card closes. A short close delay, or an invisible bridge element across the gap, fixes it. An opening delay stops a series of cards flashing as the mouse crosses a list.

Touch screens have no hover, so a tap should follow the link.

The `interestfor` attribute is an emerging way to declare this behaviour. Support is limited, so treat it as an enhancement over a normal link.
quotes: The profile preview closes before I can reach the Follow button.
The hover card closes on `mouseleave`. Add a short delay so the pointer can cross the gap.

nodes.name: Portal
nodes.description: Rendering a component's output at a different place in the DOM from where it is declared, typically at the end of body.
nodes.markdown:
A portal renders a piece of interface at a different place in the DOM from where it is declared, typically at the end of `<body>`. The code still treats it as a child of the component that owns it. Portals exist to solve a visual problem: a menu inside a [card](node:Card) gets cut off by `overflow: hidden`, or sits behind a header despite `z-index: 9999`, because an ancestor created a stacking context, a group of elements layered together. Moving the element out of that ancestor frees it.

Native features now cover many of these cases.

| Need                              | Prefer                                      |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| Modal overlay                     | `<dialog>` with `showModal()`               |
| Menu or panel above the page      | The [`popover`](node:Popover) attribute     |
| Placing it next to its trigger    | [Anchor positioning](node:Anchor%20positioning) |
| Older browser support, or a library that requires it | Portal                   |

The top layer used by `<dialog>` and popovers escapes clipping and stacking without moving the element, so it keeps its position in the DOM.

A portal's main cost is that document order and visual order diverge, and Tab and screen reader order follow the DOM. A [dropdown menu](node:Dropdown%20menu) portalled to the end of `<body>` looks adjacent to its [button](node:Button), but is reached only after everything else on the page. WCAG failure F85 describes this case. Move focus into the portalled content when it opens, return it on close, and close it when focus leaves.

Inherited CSS from the old parent stops applying, so a [theming](node:Theming) class on a wrapper is lost. In some frameworks, events still bubble through the component tree, so a click in a portalled menu can trigger a handler on a parent row.

Remove portalled nodes when the owner unmounts, or stale overlays stay on the page.
quotes: The portalled menu looks right, but Tab jumps to the page footer.
It's at the end of `body` now. Use the top layer instead so it stays in DOM order.

nodes.name: Focus trap
nodes.description: Keeping keyboard focus inside an open overlay, so Tab cycles through its controls and cannot reach the page behind it.
quotes: Screen reader users can still read the page behind our modal.
Our focus trap only handles Tab. Set `inert` on the app root while it's open.

nodes.name: Scroll lock
nodes.description: Stopping the page behind an open overlay from scrolling, without shifting the layout or losing the scroll position.
quotes: The page jumps sideways every time the modal opens.
The scroll lock removes the scrollbar. Add `scrollbar-gutter: stable` to the root.

nodes.name: Anchor positioning
nodes.description: A CSS feature that positions an element relative to another element, with fallbacks when it would overflow the viewport.
quotes: Every row's menu opens at the bottom of the table.
They all share one `anchor-name`, so anchor positioning picks the last. Add `anchor-scope` to each row.

nodes.name: Toast
nodes.description: A brief, non-blocking message that appears over the page to report a result, then usually leaves by itself.
nodes.markdown:
A toast is a brief message that appears over the page to report the result of an action, such as "Message sent", and usually leaves after a few seconds. It does not block the interface or take focus. A common failure is an "Upload failed" toast that disappears while the user is looking elsewhere, leaving no record of what went wrong. Use a toast only for information the user can afford to miss or can find again. | Message | Component | | --------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------- | | Saved, copied, sent | Toast | | Condition affecting the whole page or account | [Banner](node:Banner) | | Problem with one section | [Inline alert](node:Inline%20alert) | | Decision needed before continuing | [Alert dialog](node:Alert%20dialog) | Screen readers, which read the interface aloud, learn about toasts through a live region: an element whose changes are announced without moving focus. Keep an empty container with `role="status"` in the page from the start, then insert each message into it. A region created at the same moment as its text may not be announced. Reserve `role="alert"` for errors, because it can interrupt current speech. ```html
``` A timeout is acceptable when the same information exists elsewhere, such as a sent message appearing in the Sent folder. If the toast is the only place the information appears, WCAG 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable applies, so keep it on screen until dismissed. Pause the timer while the toast is hovered or contains focus. Actions inside toasts need a second route. Live regions usually announce content as plain text, so a screen reader user may not learn that a [button](node:Button) exists, and a keyboard user may not reach it in time. Offer any [undo](node:Undo%20pattern) from a menu, history view or shortcut as well. Queue multiple toasts and cap how many show at once.
quotes: The export error toast disappeared before I could read which file failed.
Errors should not time out. Keep it until dismissed, and list the failure on the exports page too.

nodes.name: Banner
nodes.description: A full-width message at the top of a page or region describing a condition that affects everything below it.
nodes.markdown:
A banner is a full-width message at the top of a page or region that describes a condition affecting everything below it, such as scheduled maintenance, an expired payment card or lost connectivity. It stays in the layout until the condition ends or the user dismisses it. Unlike a [toast](node:Toast), it does not time out. Unlike an [inline alert](node:Inline%20alert), it is not tied to one part of the content.

| Scope of the message              | Component                           |
| --------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| Whole product or account, ongoing | Banner                              |
| Result of one action, brief       | Toast                               |
| One section or form               | Inline alert                        |
| Must be answered to continue      | [Modal dialog](node:Modal%20dialog) |

The ARIA role named `banner` is a different thing. ARIA is a set of attributes that describe an interface to assistive technology, and `role="banner"` marks the site-wide header landmark, which a top-level `<header>` already provides. Do not put it on a notification.

A message present at page load needs no live role, because it is read in document order. A message that appears later should be inserted into an existing `role="status"` container, or `role="alert"` if urgent, so that screen readers, which read the UI aloud, announce it.

Sticky banners reduce the visible area, and on small or zoomed screens several stacked banners can fill the viewport. A sticky banner can also cover the element a keyboard user has just tabbed to, which fails WCAG 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) when that element is entirely hidden. Let banners scroll away, show one at a time, or reserve space with `scroll-padding-top`.

A dismissed banner that returns on every page load teaches users to ignore it. Store the dismissal and show the banner again only when the message changes. Keep billing or security notices visible until resolved.
quotes: Users keep closing the maintenance notice and it comes back on every route.
The banner's dismissal is only in component state. Persist it against the notice ID.

nodes.name: Inline alert
nodes.description: A message placed in the page content beside the thing it concerns, reporting information, success, a warning or an error.
nodes.markdown:
An inline alert is a message placed within the page content, next to the thing it concerns, that reports information, success, a warning or an error. Because it occupies space in the layout, it stays readable for as long as it is relevant. Use it instead of a [toast](node:Toast) when the user needs to read the message while working on that part of the page, and instead of a [banner](node:Banner) when the condition does not affect the whole page.

For forms, narrower patterns exist. [Inline validation](node:Inline%20validation) belongs to a single field, and an [error summary](node:Error%20summary) collects every error after submission. An inline alert suits a problem with the form as a whole, such as "Your payment could not be processed."

| Severity | Example                 | Role if inserted after load    |
| -------- | ----------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| Info     | Plan changes next month | `status`                       |
| Success  | Settings saved          | `status`                       |
| Warning  | API key expires today   | `status`, or `alert` if urgent |
| Error    | Payment failed          | `alert`                        |

These roles make screen readers, which read the UI aloud, announce a change without moving focus. An alert already on the page at load is generally not announced, so a static notice needs no live role and is read in document order.

Severity cannot rely on color alone, as WCAG 1.4.1 Use of Color requires another visual cue. Pair the color with an icon and a word such as "Error", and give meaningful icons a text alternative.

An error rendered at the top of a long form can appear off-screen, so the submit [button](node:Button) seems to do nothing. An alert inserted above a control can also push that control down just as the user clicks it. Render the alert near the action, reserve its space, or move focus to it after a failed submission.
quotes: Clicking Pay does nothing when the card is declined.
It does show an error, but above the fold. Move the inline alert next to the Pay button.

nodes.name: Badge
nodes.description: A small read-only label attached to another element, showing a count or short status such as 3 or Beta.
nodes.markdown: A badge is a small read-only label attached to another element that shows a count or short status, such as "3" on an inbox icon or "Beta" beside a feature name. If the user can click, remove or toggle it, use a [chip](node:Chip) instead. | Need | Component | | ----------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- | | Count or status on another element | Badge | | Removable or selectable value | Chip | | Sentence explaining a condition | [Inline alert](node:Inline%20alert) | A number alone gives little context to someone using a screen reader, software that reads the UI aloud. An inbox link containing a badge may be read as "Inbox 3", which does not say three of what. A dot badge has no text at all. Provide the meaning in text that is visually hidden but still exposed to assistive technology: ```html Inbox 3 , 3 unread messages ``` Updating a badge does not announce anything by itself. If the user needs to know about the change, such as an item being added to a cart, write a short message into a `role="status"` region, which screen readers read without moving focus. Do not announce every increment of a busy counter. Color needs two checks. Status cannot be conveyed by color alone under WCAG 1.4.1, so a red or green badge also needs a word or icon. Small text on a colored fill must still meet the 4.5:1 text contrast ratio in WCAG 1.4.3, and this is often where badges fail. A badge positioned over an icon gets clipped when an ancestor has `overflow: hidden`, and a long count can cover the icon. Cap the display at a value like `99+` while keeping the full number in the hidden text, and set a `min-width` equal to the height so single digits stay round. Hide the badge at zero, because a permanent indicator stops carrying information.
quotes: VoiceOver just says 'Notifications 12' on that button.
The badge needs hidden text saying 12 unread, otherwise the number has no meaning.

nodes.name: Progress bar
nodes.description: A track that fills to show how much of a task has finished, or that work continues when the amount is unknown.
nodes.markdown:
A progress bar is a track that fills to show how much of a task has finished. A determinate bar shows a measured value, and an indeterminate bar shows only that work is continuing. A bar that races to 99 percent and then stalls for a minute is usually driven by a timer or a poor estimate instead of measured work.

| Wait                                 | Indicator                                |
| ------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------- |
| Known amount of work                 | Determinate progress bar                 |
| Unknown length, several seconds+     | Indeterminate bar with status text       |
| Short and unknown                    | [Spinner](node:Spinner)                  |
| Content with a known layout          | [Skeleton screen](node:Skeleton%20screen) |

Use the native `<progress>` element where possible. Removing its `value` attribute makes it indeterminate. With a custom `role="progressbar"`, omit `aria-valuenow` for the same result. The bar needs an accessible name, and text between the `<progress>` tags is only a fallback, not a label.

```html
<label for="upload">Uploading report.pdf</label>
<progress id="upload" value="40" max="100">40%</progress>
```

A screen reader, which reads the UI aloud, should not speak every percentage. Announce milestones, such as each quarter and completion, in a separate `role="status"` region. When the bar reports on a page region, set `aria-busy="true"` on that region and clear it when loading ends, including when it fails, because assistive technology may hold back changes while it is set.

Several failures are common. The bar jumps backward when a second stage resets the value, so combine stages into one total or label them "Step 2 of 3". The bar freezes at 62 percent after a failure, so switch it to a visible [error state](node:Error%20state) with a retry. Long tasks also need a way to cancel.

Use `<meter>` instead for a measurement that is not a task, such as disk usage.
quotes: The upload sits at 100 percent for ages before it finishes.
That progress bar only tracks bytes sent. Add a processing stage so it doesn't claim to be done early.

nodes.name: Spinner
nodes.description: A looping animation showing that work is in progress without saying how much remains.
nodes.markdown:
A spinner is a looping animation that shows work is in progress without saying how much remains. It suits short waits of unknown length, such as a [button](node:Button) submitting a form. A spinner that never stops usually means the request failed and the code has no path out of its loading state. | Situation | Indicator | | --------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- | | Short wait, unknown length | Spinner | | Measurable work | [Progress bar](node:Progress%20bar) | | Content with a predictable layout | [Skeleton screen](node:Skeleton%20screen) | | Action almost certain to succeed | [Optimistic UI](node:Optimistic%20UI) | An animation conveys nothing to a screen reader, which reads the UI aloud. Add text such as "Loading results" to a `role="status"` region that already exists in the page, so the message is announced without moving focus. Hide the decorative graphic with `aria-hidden="true"`. ```html
Loading results
``` Spinners inside a button have their own problems. Replacing the label changes the button's width and removes its accessible name, so keep the label in place and overlay the graphic. Setting `disabled` during the request can drop keyboard focus. Use `aria-disabled="true"` and ignore repeat clicks instead. On a fast response, a spinner appears as a brief flicker, so delay it by a few hundred milliseconds. Once shown, keep it visible briefly so it does not flash. Add a timeout that leads to an [error state](node:Error%20state). Under WCAG 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide, moving content that runs for more than five seconds alongside other content needs a way to stop it, unless the movement is essential. A preloader that is the only content on the page is not in that position. For long waits beside usable content, show text instead. Under [reduced motion](node:Reduced%20motion), replace rotation with a slow opacity change.
quotes: The dashboard spinner has been going for ten minutes.
The fetch rejected and nothing clears the loading flag. It needs a timeout and an error state.

nodes.name: Skeleton screen
nodes.description: A placeholder that shows grey shapes in the layout of the coming content while the real data loads.
nodes.markdown:
A skeleton screen is a placeholder that shows grey shapes in the layout of the coming content while the real data loads. Because the shapes hold the space the content will use, the page does not jump when data arrives. It suits content regions whose structure is known in advance, such as a feed, profile or [data table](node:Data%20table). | Situation | Indicator | | ---------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- | | Known layout, loading content | Skeleton screen | | [Button](node:Button) or small inline wait | [Spinner](node:Spinner) | | Long task with measurable progress | [Progress bar](node:Progress%20bar) | | Response usually instant | No indicator | A skeleton that does not match the final layout causes the jump it was meant to prevent. If it shows three lines and the content has five, everything below shifts on load. Build skeletons from the same layout as the real component, and give images a reserved size with [aspect ratio](node:Aspect%20ratio). The shapes mean nothing to a screen reader, which reads the UI aloud, so hide them with `aria-hidden="true"`. Announce loading through a short message in a `role="status"` region. You can set `aria-busy="true"` on the region being replaced, which asks assistive technology to wait for the update to finish. Clear it on success and on failure. ```html

Orders

``` Shimmer animations need the same care as other motion. Stop or soften them under [reduced motion](node:Reduced%20motion), and remember that WCAG 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide applies to movement lasting over five seconds alongside other content unless it is essential. Two other failures are common. A request that fails can leave the skeleton in place forever, so every loading path needs an [error state](node:Error%20state). A skeleton shown for a fast response flashes on screen, so delay it briefly or skip it for cached data.
quotes: The orders page jumps about a second after it loads.
The skeleton has fixed rows but the real rows wrap to two lines. Match the row height.

nodes.name: Empty state
nodes.description: The content shown when a view has nothing to display, explaining why and what the user can do next.
nodes.markdown:
An empty state is the content shown when a view has nothing to display, explaining why and what the user can do next. Without one, a new user opens a project list and sees a blank area, with no way to tell whether the page is broken, still loading or empty.

The right message depends on why the view is empty.

| Cause               | Example message            | Next action     |
| ------------------- | -------------------------- | --------------- |
| First use           | "No projects yet"          | Create project  |
| No search results   | "No results for 'invoce'"  | Clear search    |
| Filters too narrow  | "No open tickets match"    | Reset filters   |
| Work completed      | "All caught up"            | None needed     |
| No permission       | "You don't have access"    | Request access  |

Keep empty, loading and failed as three separate states. A common bug is initialising the list to `[]`, which renders "No invoices" for a moment before the data arrives. A worse one is falling back to `[]` when the request fails, which tells users their data is gone. Track request status explicitly and show an [error state](node:Error%20state) for failures and a [skeleton screen](node:Skeleton%20screen) while loading.

For accessibility, use real text and a real heading or paragraph. Illustrations are usually decorative here, so give them `alt=""`. When a search or filter empties the results without a page load, announce the outcome through a `role="status"` region that already exists, such as "No results found". WCAG 4.1.3 Status Messages covers this kind of update, which should reach screen readers (software that reads the UI aloud) without moving focus.

Keep the message specific and offer one primary action. When filters caused the empty result, repeat the active filters so the user can see what to change. Do not fill the space with marketing copy on a screen where someone is trying to work.
quotes: A customer thought we deleted their invoices.
The API timed out and we rendered the empty state. A failed fetch needs its own error state.

nodes.name: Error state
nodes.description: The content shown when data or an action fails, saying what happened and how the user can recover.
nodes.markdown:
An error state is the content shown when data or an action fails, saying what happened and how the user can recover. A generic "Something went wrong" with no next step leaves the user unable to tell whether to retry, wait or contact support.

Match the size of the error to the size of the failure, so one broken widget does not take down the page.

| Scope                 | Treatment                                       |
| --------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- |
| One field             | [Inline validation](node:Inline%20validation)   |
| A submitted form      | [Error summary](node:Error%20summary)           |
| One section or widget | [Inline alert](node:Inline%20alert) with retry  |
| Whole product degraded | [Banner](node:Banner)                          |
| Page cannot render    | Full-page error with navigation still available |

A useful error state answers three questions: what failed, whether the user's work is safe, and what to do next. "We couldn't load your invoices. Your data is safe. Try again." is more useful than a status code. Distinguish causes when you can, because being offline, lacking permission and a server fault each call for a different action.

Keep it distinct from an [empty state](node:Empty%20state). Code that catches a failed request and returns an empty list makes an outage look like missing data.

Preserve what the user entered. A retry that clears a long form turns a small failure into lost work.

For accessibility, an error that appears after an action should reach screen readers, which read the UI aloud. Insert it into a `role="alert"` region, which announces it without moving focus. When a whole view is replaced by the error, move focus to its heading by giving the heading `tabindex="-1"` and calling `.focus()`, otherwise focus can be lost with the removed content. Do not signal the error with red alone, since WCAG 1.4.1 Use of Color requires another cue such as an icon or text.
quotes: When the reports API fails, the whole dashboard goes blank.
Wrap each widget so a failure shows a local error state with a retry button.

nodes.name: Undo pattern
nodes.description: Applying an action immediately and offering a way to reverse it, instead of asking for confirmation first.
nodes.markdown:
The undo pattern applies an action immediately and offers a way to reverse it, instead of asking for confirmation first. Archiving an email and seeing "Conversation archived. Undo" is the typical example. It avoids the confirmation prompts that users learn to click through without reading.

Choose between undo and confirmation based on whether the action can actually be reversed.

| Action                              | Approach                            |
| ----------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| Frequent and reversible             | Undo                                |
| Destructive but recoverable         | Undo, backed by a trash or history  |
| Irreversible, or affects other people | [Alert dialog](node:Alert%20dialog) confirmation |
| Payment or legal commitment         | Review step before submitting       |

WCAG 3.3.4 Error Prevention (Legal, Financial, Data) applies to pages that create legal or financial commitments, or that change or delete user-controllable data. Those submissions must be reversible, checked for errors, or confirmed, so undo is one valid way to meet it.

There are three common implementations:

| Method           | How it works                         | Weakness                                  |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------- |
| Delayed commit   | Send the request when the window ends | Closing the tab can lose or skip the action |
| Soft delete      | Mark as deleted, purge later         | Needs storage and a cleanup job           |
| Inverse action   | Run the opposite operation           | Fails if later changes conflict           |

The usual failure is an undo offered only in a [toast](node:Toast). If the toast times out, the option disappears, and a keyboard user or someone on a screen reader (software that reads the UI aloud) may never reach it. Keep a lasting route as well, such as a Trash view, an activity history or a keyboard shortcut.

Undo must also restore the full previous state, including the item's position in its list. Return focus to the restored item or a sensible neighbour, because the element that had focus may have been removed. Announce both the action and its reversal through a `role="status"` region.
quotes: Should deleting a label ask 'Are you sure?'
No, it's easy to reverse. Use the undo pattern, and keep deleted labels recoverable for 30 days.

nodes.name: Optimistic UI
nodes.description: Showing the result of an action immediately, before the server confirms it, and rolling back if the request fails.
nodes.markdown:
Optimistic UI shows the result of an action immediately, before the server confirms it, and rolls back if the request fails. A like [button](node:Button) that fills on tap, while the request runs in the background, is the typical example. It removes the visible wait on actions that almost always succeed.

| Step | Who    | What happens                                |
| ---- | ------ | ------------------------------------------- |
| 1    | User   | Triggers the action                         |
| 2    | Client | Saves the previous state and updates the UI |
| 3    | Client | Sends the request                           |
| 4    | Server | Accepts or rejects it                       |
| 5    | Client | On success, reconciles with the response    |
| 6    | Client | On failure, restores state and tells the user |

Use it for frequent, low-stakes, reversible actions such as starring, reordering or renaming. Do not use it for payments, permission changes or anything where showing success falsely would mislead someone. For those, show a pending state with a [spinner](node:Spinner) until the server confirms.

A silent rollback is a common failure. The user likes a post, moves on, and later finds the like has vanished because the request failed and nothing said so. Every rollback needs a message, usually a [toast](node:Toast) or [inline alert](node:Inline%20alert) with a retry.

Race conditions are the second failure. If a user toggles a star on and off quickly, responses can arrive out of order and leave the wrong final state. Cancel earlier requests, or ignore any response that is not the latest for that item. Retried requests can also create duplicates, so give each create operation a client-generated ID the server can deduplicate.

Assistive technology needs the same truth as the screen. Update states such as `aria-pressed` immediately, and when a rollback occurs, announce it through a `role="alert"` region, because a state that silently reverts is otherwise easy to miss.
quotes: Comments sometimes appear twice after a flaky connection.
The optimistic UI retries without an idempotency key. Generate an ID on the client so the server can dedupe.

nodes.name: Card
nodes.description: A bounded container that groups content and actions about one item, usually repeated in a grid or list.
nodes.markdown:
A card is a bounded container that groups content and actions about one item, such as a product, article or team member. Cards are usually repeated in a grid or list so people can scan separate items. If people need to compare the same attribute across many items, use a [data table](node:Data%20table), because aligned columns make comparison easier than scattered card fields.

| Content                              | Component  |
| ------------------------------------ | ---------- |
| Separate items with mixed content    | Card       |
| Many records compared by attribute   | Data table |
| Simple items with one line each      | List       |
| One group of related settings        | Plain section with a heading |

Clickable cards are where most problems occur. Wrapping the entire card in `<a>` makes a screen reader (software that reads the UI aloud) announce all of its content as one long link name, and placing a [button](node:Button) inside that link creates invalid nested interactive elements. A safer pattern keeps the link on the heading and stretches its hit area over the card with a pseudo-element:

```css
.card { position: relative; }
.card h3 a::after { content: ""; position: absolute; inset: 0; }
.card button { position: relative; z-index: 1; }
```

The raised `z-index` keeps secondary buttons clickable above the stretched link. The trade-off is that text in the card becomes harder to select, because the overlay receives the pointer.

Use semantic structure inside the card. Give each one a real heading at the correct level for the page, and mark a repeated set as a list with `<ul>`.

Uneven content is the common visual failure. One long title makes a card taller and misaligns the buttons in its row. Put cards in a grid so they stretch to equal height, make each card a flex column, and push the actions to the bottom with `margin-top: auto`. Reserve image space with [aspect ratio](node:Aspect%20ratio) to prevent shifts as images load.
quotes: The screen reader reads the entire product card as one link.
Move the link onto the card's title and stretch it with a pseudo-element.

nodes.name: Data table
nodes.description: Rows and columns of structured records, built so people can read, compare, sort and act on them.
nodes.markdown:
A data table presents structured records in rows and columns so people can read, compare, sort and act on them. Use it when each row has the same fields and people need to compare values down a column. For a small set of items with varied content, a [card](node:Card) or list is usually easier to scan. Build it with a native ``, which gives screen readers (software that reads the UI aloud) row and column relationships for free. A table made of `
` elements announces no headers unless every role is added by hand. ```html
Open invoices
Amount
``` Put a [button](node:Button) inside each sortable header and set `aria-sort` on the `` of the sorted column. | Content | Pattern | | ------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- | | Static data, few controls | Table | | Many interactive cells, spreadsheet-like | Grid, with arrow-key movement | The WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices recommend a grid when a table holds many widgets, because a grid has one Tab stop and arrow keys move between cells. It takes significant work, so do not adopt it for a table with one link per row. Wide tables are the common failure on small screens. Wrap the table in a scrolling container so the page itself does not overflow. Some browsers do not make scrolling regions keyboard-focusable, so add `tabindex="0"`, `role="region"` and an `aria-label` to it. WCAG 1.4.10 Reflow allows data tables to scroll in two dimensions, but the headings, search and [pagination](node:Pagination%20control) around them must still reflow. For long data, use pagination or a [virtualized list](node:Virtualized%20list). If rows are missing from the DOM, set `aria-rowcount` to the total and `aria-rowindex` on each row. Keep column headers visible with a [sticky header](node:Sticky%20header).
quotes: Keyboard users have to tab through 400 links in the orders list.
That's a data table acting like a grid. Use the grid pattern, or reduce it to one link per row.

nodes.name: Sticky header
nodes.description: A header that scrolls with the page until it reaches an edge, then stays visible while content moves beneath it.
quotes: The table header stopped sticking after the redesign.
The new wrapper has `overflow: hidden`, so that's now the sticky header's scroll container.

nodes.name: Row selection
nodes.description: Letting users mark one or more rows in a table or list so a bulk action can apply to them.
nodes.markdown:
Row selection lets users mark one or more rows in a [data table](node:Data%20table) or list so an action can apply to all of them, such as archiving twenty invoices at once. It usually appears as a [checkbox](node:Checkbox) column, with a header checkbox for selecting all rows and a [toolbar](node:Toolbar) showing the bulk actions.

The header checkbox has three states, and `indeterminate` is set from script because HTML has no attribute for it.

| Rows selected | Header checkbox                           |
| ------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| None          | Unchecked                                 |
| Some          | Indeterminate (`aria-checked="mixed"`)    |
| All           | Checked                                   |

An unclear "select all" can cause data loss. On a paginated table, a user ticks the header, sees every visible row checked and presses Delete, unsure whether that means 25 rows or all 1,240. State the scope in text ("25 selected. Select all 1,240") and make the larger selection a separate step. Confirm destructive bulk actions with an [alert dialog](node:Alert%20dialog) that repeats the count.

Store selection by record ID and never by row index. Index-based selection attaches to the wrong records as soon as the table is sorted, filtered or paged.

Each checkbox needs a distinct accessible name, such as "Select invoice 1042". A column of checkboxes all named "Select" gives someone using a screen reader, which reads the UI aloud, no way to tell them apart. Announce the running count through a `role="status"` region.

| Structure                     | How selection is exposed            |
| ----------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| Native table with checkboxes  | The checkbox state                  |
| Grid widget (`role="grid"`)   | `aria-selected` on the row or cell  |

In a grid, the WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices require the selected state to look different from the focus indicator, and moving focus in a multi-select grid should not change the selection. If clicking a row also opens it, keep the checkbox as a separate target so that selecting does not navigate.
quotes: Sorting by date changed which rows were selected.
We're tracking row selection by index. Key it on the invoice ID.

nodes.name: Virtualized list
nodes.description: A long list that renders only the rows near the viewport and swaps them as the user scrolls.
nodes.markdown:
A virtualized list renders only the rows near the viewport and swaps them as the user scrolls, while a spacer keeps the scrollbar the correct size for the full list. A list of 50,000 rows might have only 30 in the DOM at any moment. Without it, a very long list can make the page slow to render and scroll. Virtualization has real costs, so try simpler options first. | Option | Keeps rows in DOM | Find-in-page | Suits | | -------------------------- | ----------------- | ------------ | ------------------------ | | [Pagination](node:Pagination%20control) | Current page only | Current page | Most business data | | `content-visibility: auto` | Yes | Yes | Long pages, moderate lists | | Virtualization | Visible rows only | Rendered rows only | Very large lists | The CSS `content-visibility: auto` property skips rendering for off-screen content while leaving it available to find-in-page and the Tab order. Removing rows from the DOM causes the failures people notice. Pressing Ctrl+F does not find a row that is not rendered, so provide a [search field](node:Search%20field). Scrolling quickly can show blank space until rows mount, which rendering a few extra rows reduces. Rows of varying height can make the scroll position jump when estimates are corrected, so measure them or use a fixed height. Focus is the main accessibility risk. If the focused row scrolls out and unmounts, focus falls to the document body and a keyboard user loses their place. Keep the focused row mounted, or restore focus when it returns. Screen readers, which read the UI aloud, only see what is in the DOM, so state the true size: ```html
  • Ada Moreno
  • Ben Okafor
``` For tables, use `aria-rowcount` on the table and `aria-rowindex` on each row. Use stable item IDs as keys, since reusing a row by index can leak state such as a checked box into a different record.
quotes: Ctrl+F can't find a customer I can see further down the list.
It's a virtualized list, so that row isn't in the DOM. We need a search box.

nodes.name: Infinite scroll
nodes.description: A list that loads and appends more items automatically as the user nears the end.
nodes.markdown:
Infinite scroll loads and appends more items automatically as the user nears the end of a list. It is usually triggered by an `IntersectionObserver`, a browser API that reports when a marker element near the bottom comes into view. It suits feeds that people browse without a specific target, and it works poorly when people need to find, compare or return to a particular item. | Pattern | Position shareable | Footer reachable | Suits | | ------------------------------------------- | ------------------ | ---------------- | ------------------ | | [Pagination](node:Pagination%20control) | Yes | Yes | Search, records | | Load more [button](node:Button) | With extra work | Yes | Product listings | | Infinite scroll | With extra work | No, unless moved | Social-style feeds | Several failures are characteristic. The footer keeps moving away as items load, so its links cannot be clicked. Opening an item and pressing Back returns the user to the top of the list. Memory grows as thousands of items accumulate, which a [virtualized list](node:Virtualized%20list) can address. To restore position, store the page or item in the URL with `history.replaceState` and reload that slice on return. People using a keyboard or a screen reader, which reads the UI aloud, face a further problem. Content that loads as focus moves can trap them in the list, unable to reach anything after it. A "Load more" button avoids this, because the user decides when content is added. If you do build a feed, the WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices define a `feed` pattern: ```html
...
``` Use `aria-setsize="-1"` when the total is unknown. Set `aria-busy="true"` while articles are being added and return it to `false` afterwards. The pattern recommends Page Down and Page Up to move between articles, and Control+End to move past the feed. Announce loading and the end of the list through a `role="status"` region, and never remove the item that has focus.
quotes: I can't click Privacy in the footer because the page keeps growing.
That's infinite scroll pushing it away. Switch to a Load more button.

nodes.name: Accordion
nodes.description: A vertical stack of headers that each expand or collapse a section of content.
nodes.markdown:
An accordion is a vertical stack of headers that each expand or collapse a section of content. It shortens long pages where people need only some sections, such as an FAQ or a settings list. If people need to read most of the content, leave it expanded, because collapsed sections add clicks and hide text from a quick scan. | Need | Component | | -------------------------------------- | ------------------------ | | Several optional sections, stacked | Accordion | | Peer views, one visible at a time | [Tabs](node:Tabs) | | One show or hide control | Disclosure (`
`) | | Content everyone must read | Plain headings | The WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices define the structure. Each header is a real [button](node:Button) inside a heading, and the button is the only element in that heading. The button carries `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls`. Enter and Space toggle the panel, and Tab moves through the page as usual. ```html

Orders leave within two days.
``` A panel can also take `role="region"` with `aria-labelledby` pointing at its button. Avoid this when many panels can be open at once, roughly more than six, because it adds too many landmarks for people using a screen reader, which reads the UI aloud, to navigate. Native `
` elements sharing the same `name` attribute form an exclusive group with no script, so opening one closes the others. Test it with a screen reader. Single-open behaviour can move content away from the pointer. When a user opens a lower section, the open section above collapses, the content shifts up, and the header they clicked can move out of view. Allow several panels open, or scroll the opened header back into view. Text in a collapsed panel may not appear in find-in-page, so test it and offer an "Expand all" control on long pages. Animate height only when [reduced motion](node:Reduced%20motion) is not requested.
quotes: Opening question eight jumps the page and I lose my place.
The accordion closes question three above it. Let multiple panels stay open.

nodes.name: Carousel
nodes.description: A region that shows one slide or a few items at a time, with controls for moving through the rest.
nodes.markdown:
A carousel is a region that shows one slide or a few items at a time, with controls for moving through the rest. It saves vertical space, but content on later slides is easy to miss, and a slide that advances while someone is reading takes the text away from them. If every item matters, a stacked list or a grid of [cards](node:Card) keeps all of it visible. | Need | Component | | --------------------------------- | ----------------------------- | | All items must be seen | Grid or list | | Browse similar items sideways | Scroll container with snap | | Gallery of images | Thumbnails and [lightbox](node:Lightbox) | | Rotating promotional slides | Carousel with a stop control | Auto-rotation carries the strictest requirements. WCAG 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide requires a way to pause moving content that starts automatically, lasts more than five seconds and appears alongside other content. The WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices add specific behaviour: | Requirement | Behaviour | | ---------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- | | Rotation control | A [button](node:Button) to stop and restart, first in the Tab sequence | | Pointer hover | Rotation stops while hovering | | Keyboard focus | Rotation stops when focus enters, until explicitly restarted | | Live region | `aria-live="off"` while rotating, `polite` when stopped | | Next, Previous | Buttons that keep focus in place when activated | ```html
...
``` Hidden slides are a common accessibility bug. If off-screen slides stay focusable, Tab moves focus to links the user cannot see. Apply the `inert` attribute or `hidden` to inactive slides. Touch-only swiping is another gap. WCAG 2.5.7 Dragging Movements requires a single-pointer alternative, so visible Next and Previous buttons are needed. If you set `touch-action`, keep vertical panning and pinch zoom available, for example with `pan-y pinch-zoom`. Also honour [reduced motion](node:Reduced%20motion) by disabling auto-rotation and sliding transitions.
quotes: The hero slide changes while I'm still reading it.
The carousel needs to stop on hover and focus, and it needs a visible pause button.

nodes.name: Avatar
nodes.description: A small image, initials or icon that represents a person or account in an interface.
nodes.markdown: An avatar is a small image, set of initials or icon that represents a person or account. It helps people recognise who wrote a comment, who owns a task or which account is signed in. A fallback chain prevents the broken-image icon that appears when a photo URL fails. | Priority | Display | When | | -------- | ----------------- | ----------------------------- | | 1 | Photo | Image loads successfully | | 2 | Initials | No image, or loading failed | | 3 | Generic icon | No name available | The correct alt text depends on what sits next to the image. When the person's name is adjacent, the avatar repeats it, so use `alt=""` and screen readers, which read the UI aloud, skip it. When the avatar stands alone, the alt text should be the person's name. Do not use "avatar" or "profile picture" as alt text. ```html Priya Shah ``` Uploaded photos are rarely square, and stretching them distorts faces. Set equal width and height attributes to reserve the space and prevent layout shift, then crop with `object-fit: cover`. For a shape that scales, use [aspect ratio](node:Aspect%20ratio). Initials fallbacks have their own traps. Names do not always split into a first and last name, so derive initials carefully and handle single names and non-Latin scripts. Background colors generated from a hash can produce unreadable combinations, so choose from a fixed palette that meets the 4.5:1 text contrast ratio. An avatar that opens an account menu is a control, so wrap it in a real [button](node:Button) with a name such as "Account menu". Its [touch target](node:Touch%20target) should meet WCAG 2.5.8, which asks for 24 by 24 CSS pixels or enough spacing around a smaller target. A stack of overlapping avatars can fail both. In a group, summarise the overflow with a "+3" item whose accessible name says "3 more members".
quotes: Half the comment avatars are showing a broken image icon.
Those users have expired photo URLs. Fall back to initials on the image error event.

nodes.name: Chip
nodes.description: A compact interactive element representing a value, filter or choice that can be selected or removed.
nodes.markdown:
A chip is a compact interactive element that represents a value, filter or choice, usually drawn as a rounded pill. Selecting "In stock" on a product page or removing a recipient from an email field are typical uses. A [badge](node:Badge) looks similar but is read-only, so the deciding question is whether the user can act on it. Chips cover several behaviours, and each needs different markup. | Type | Purpose | Semantics | | ---------- | --------------------- | ------------------------------- | | Filter | Turns a filter on/off | [Button](node:Button) with `aria-pressed`, or a [checkbox](node:Checkbox) | | Choice | Pick one of a set | Radio inputs | | Input | A value the user added | Text plus a remove button | | Suggestion | Run an action | Plain button | For a value the user entered, as in a [tag input](node:Tag%20input), the chip is text with a separate remove button. That button needs a specific name, because a list of buttons all announced as "Remove" or "×" does not say what each one removes. ```html
  • Design
    • ``` The small remove icon often fails on size. WCAG 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) requires pointer targets of at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, unless spacing or another exception applies. Extend the hit area with padding or a pseudo-element, without enlarging the icon, so users do not delete the wrong chip with a slightly misplaced tap. Removing a chip destroys the element that had focus, and focus can fall back to the top of the page. Move focus to the next chip, or to the input when none remain, and report the removal in a `role="status"` region. Selected state must not rely on color alone under WCAG 1.4.1, so add a check mark or a change in border. A group of filter chips needs a label, using `role="group"` with `aria-label` or a `
    `.
quotes: After deleting a filter, Tab starts from the top of the page again.
The chip had focus when it was removed. Move focus to the next chip.

nodes.name: Timeline
nodes.description: A chronological display of events along a line, showing what happened and when.
nodes.markdown:
A timeline is a chronological display of events along a line, showing what happened and when. Order histories, audit logs, incident reports and account activity commonly use one. A [stepper](node:Stepper) looks similar but shows progress through a defined process with future steps, while a timeline mainly records events that have already occurred. | Need | Component | | ------------------------------------ | ---------------- | | Record of past events | Timeline | | Progress through known steps | Stepper | | Records compared by field | [Data table](node:Data%20table) | | Stream of incoming messages | Log (`role="log"`) | Use an ordered list, because sequence is the meaning of the component. Mark each date with `` so the machine-readable value is available, and add the `reversed` attribute when the newest event comes first so the numbering stays correct. ```html
  1. 14 Mar, 09:30 UTC Order shipped
  2. 13 Mar, 16:05 UTC Payment received
``` Draw the connecting line and dots with CSS pseudo-elements so they stay out of the accessibility tree. If a dot's color signals a status such as failed or completed, add text or an icon as well, since WCAG 1.4.1 does not allow color to be the only cue. Date handling is where timelines usually go wrong. "2 days ago" is easy to scan but useless in an audit or a support call, so show the absolute time as well. Decide which timezone is displayed and label it. Without that, two people comparing an incident can read the same event as different times. Rendering relative or local time on the server can also produce a different value from the browser's, causing a mismatch when the page becomes interactive. Long histories need [pagination](node:Pagination%20control) or a "Show earlier" [button](node:Button), plus grouping by day. If events arrive live, avoid moving content while someone reads it. Add new entries through a notice such as "3 new events", and let the user choose when to load them.
quotes: Support and the customer disagree about when the refund happened.
The timeline only says 'yesterday'. Show the exact time and timezone on each event.

nodes.name: Kanban board
nodes.description: A board of columns representing workflow stages, with cards that move between them as work progresses.
nodes.markdown:
A kanban board is a set of columns representing workflow stages, with [cards](node:Card) that move between them as work progresses. A typical board has To do, In progress and Done. If people mainly need to sort, filter or edit many fields, a [data table](node:Data%20table) is a better default. The structure is a list of lists. Each column is a labelled section containing a list of cards, which gives screen readers (software that reads the UI aloud) the column name and item count. ```html

In progress (3)

  • Fix invoice rounding
``` [Drag and drop](node:Drag%20and%20drop) is the expected way to move cards, but it cannot be the only way. WCAG 2.5.7 Dragging Movements requires a single-pointer alternative, and a keyboard method alone does not satisfy it. A "Move to" [dropdown menu](node:Dropdown%20menu) on each card works for pointer, keyboard and screen reader users together. | Input | How a card moves | | ------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------- | | Mouse, touch | Drag to a column, or use the "Move to" menu | | Keyboard | Open the menu, or pick up with Space and move with arrows | | Screen reader | Use the menu and hear "Moved to Done, position 2" | Announce each move through a `role="status"` region, and keep focus on the moved card. Persistence causes the less visible failures. If position is stored as an integer index, one move rewrites every card below it, and two people moving cards at once can overwrite each other.
