A sortable rank value between neighbours changes only the moved card. Moves are usually [optimistic](node:Optimistic%20UI), so a rejected request must return the card to its column and say why. On narrow screens, the columns exceed the viewport. Horizontal scrolling is acceptable for the board, but dragging near an edge then needs auto-scroll. A single-column view with a stage picker often works better on phones.
quotes: Two of us moved cards and the order came back scrambled.
The kanban board saves integer positions. Switch to a rank between neighbours.

nodes.name: Lightbox
nodes.description: A full-screen overlay that shows an enlarged image or media item above a dimmed page.
nodes.markdown: A lightbox is a full-screen overlay that shows an enlarged image or media item above a dimmed page. It is a specialised [modal dialog](node:Modal%20dialog), so it inherits the same focus and dismissal rules. For a simple image, a link to the full-size file may be enough, and it works without script. | Need | Component | | ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------- | | Inspect one image closely | Lightbox, or link to the file | | Step through a gallery | Lightbox with Next and Previous | | Browse items inline | [Carousel](node:Carousel) | | Short preview on hover | [Hover card](node:Hover%20card) | The thumbnail must be a real control. An `` with a click handler cannot be reached by keyboard, so wrap it in a [button](node:Button) or link whose name describes the action. ```html ``` Opening a native `` with `showModal()` moves focus inside it, makes the rest of the page inert, closes on Escape and returns focus to the thumbnail. A custom overlay has to build each of those itself, along with a [focus trap](node:Focus%20trap). Add a [scroll lock](node:Scroll%20lock) so that the page does not move behind the image. Galleries need labelled Next and Previous buttons, plus Left and Right arrow keys as a convenience. Announce the position, such as "Image 3 of 12", in a `role="status"` region, and update the alt text with each image. Swiping cannot be the only way to move, because WCAG 2.5.7 Dragging Movements requires a single-pointer alternative. Blocked zoom is a common failure. Viewing detail is the reason to open a lightbox, yet custom touch handlers or `touch-action: none` can block pinch zoom. Keep pinch zoom working, and show a visible Close button, since not every user knows that Escape or a backdrop click will dismiss it. Under [reduced motion](node:Reduced%20motion), replace zoom transitions with a fade.
quotes: On my phone I can't pinch to see the floor plan detail.
The lightbox sets `touch-action: none`. Let the browser handle pinch zoom.

nodes.name: App shell
nodes.description: The persistent frame of an application, such as header and navigation, around a content area that changes.
quotes: The bottom nav is hidden behind Safari's toolbar on iPhones.
The app shell uses `100vh`. Switch it to `100dvh` and pad for the [safe area](node:Safe%20area).

nodes.name: Layout container
nodes.description: A centred wrapper that limits content to a maximum width and keeps consistent gutters at the page edges.
nodes.markdown:
A layout container is a centred wrapper that limits content to a maximum width and keeps consistent gutters at the page edges. Without one, text on a wide monitor stretches into lines that are tiring to read, and content on a phone touches the screen edge. The name is easy to confuse with a container query, a CSS feature that styles elements based on the size of an ancestor. A layout container only constrains width.

```css
.container {
  width: min(100% - 2rem, 70rem);
  margin-inline: auto;
}
```

The element takes the full width minus the gutters until it reaches `70rem`, then stays there and centres.

Most systems define a few widths for different content.

| Size   | Typical limit | Use                     |
| ------ | ------------- | ----------------------- |
| Prose  | `65ch`        | Articles, documentation |
| Narrow | `40rem`       | Forms, settings         |
| Wide   | `70rem`       | Dashboards, marketing   |
| Full   | None          | Tables, maps, media     |

The `ch` unit is the width of the font's zero character.

Full-width sections inside a container are a common failure. Developers often break a band out of the container with `width: 100vw`. On systems with classic scrollbars, `100vw` can be wider than the visible area, because it does not subtract the scrollbar, and the page gains a horizontal scrollbar. Avoid this by placing the band outside the container, with an inner container for its content.

Nesting containers also causes trouble. Two nested wrappers apply the gutter twice, leaving content indented on mobile. Keep one container per band of the page, and use a [stack layout](node:Stack%20layout) or grid inside it.

Avoid fixed widths. A `width: 1200px` wrapper forces horizontal scrolling on narrow or zoomed screens, and WCAG 1.4.10 Reflow requires content to fit a width equivalent to 320 CSS pixels without two-dimensional scrolling, aside from content that needs it. Let the container shrink and change the inner layout at a [breakpoint](node:Breakpoint).
quotes: There's a horizontal scrollbar on every page on Windows.
The hero uses `100vw` inside the layout container. Move it out and let it fill the body.

nodes.name: Stack layout
nodes.description: A layout that places children in one direction with a consistent gap between them.
nodes.markdown:
A stack layout places its children in one direction, vertically or horizontally, with a consistent gap between them. It covers [form fields](node:Form%20field), [card](node:Card) contents and [button](node:Button) rows. The parent controls spacing, so individual children do not need margins and can be reused anywhere.

```css
.stack {
  display: flex;
  flex-direction: column;
  gap: 1rem;
}
```

Spacing on the parent solves a recurring bug. When each child carries its own `margin-bottom`, the last child adds unwanted space at the end of its container, and adjacent vertical margins can collapse into one. A `gap` applies only between items.

| Need                               | Layout                     |
| ---------------------------------- | -------------------------- |
| One direction, even spacing        | Stack                      |
| Row that wraps onto new lines      | Flex with `flex-wrap`      |
| Items aligned in rows and columns  | Grid                       |
| Uneven heights packed in columns   | [Masonry layout](node:Masonry%20layout) |

Take gap values from a [spacing scale](node:Spacing%20scale).

An empty child still receives a gap. If a conditional wrapper renders an empty `<div>`, the stack shows a double space with nothing in it. Render nothing instead of an empty element, or apply `.stack > :empty { display: none; }` where that is safe.

Long content is another common failure. Flex items have an automatic minimum size based on their content, so a long URL in a horizontal stack can overflow instead of shrinking. Set `min-width: 0` on the item that should shrink.

Reversing visual order creates an accessibility problem. `flex-direction: column-reverse` and the `order` property move items on screen but leave the DOM order unchanged, so Tab and screen readers (software that reads the UI aloud) follow a different sequence from what is displayed. WCAG 2.4.3 Focus Order requires a sequence that preserves meaning, and 1.3.2 Meaningful Sequence requires a correct reading order where order affects meaning. If the order needs to change at a [breakpoint](node:Breakpoint), check that both sequences still make sense.
quotes: There's a strange double gap above the submit button.
A hidden field wrapper is still rendering in the stack layout. Don't render it at all.

nodes.name: Split pane
nodes.description: Two adjacent regions separated by a movable divider that lets the user resize them.
nodes.markdown:
A split pane is two adjacent regions separated by a movable divider that lets the user resize them. Code editors, email clients and design tools use it to show a list beside a detail view. Use it when people work across both regions and prefer different proportions. If one fixed ratio works for everyone, a plain two-column grid is simpler. For a panel needed only occasionally, a [drawer](node:Drawer) leaves more room for the main content. The divider is a real control. The WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices define it as the window splitter pattern, using a focusable `separator` whose value is the size of the primary pane. ```html
``` | Key | Behaviour | | ----------------- | ------------------------------------------ | | Left, Right Arrow | Move a vertical splitter | | Up, Down Arrow | Move a horizontal splitter | | Enter | Collapse the primary pane, or restore it | | Home (optional) | Give the primary pane its smallest size | | End (optional) | Give the primary pane its largest size | | F6 (optional) | Cycle between panes | WCAG 2.5.7 Dragging Movements requires a single-pointer alternative to dragging, so add collapse or step [buttons](node:Button) that can be clicked or tapped. The visible divider is often 1px wide, so extend its hit area to meet the [touch target](node:Touch%20target) requirement. A drag can stop following the cursor when the pointer leaves the divider. Call `setPointerCapture()` on pointer down so that later events keep going to the divider. If a pane contains an iframe, test dragging across it, because the frame can receive the pointer events. Setting `pointer-events: none` on the frame during the drag is a common fix. Clamp sizes so neither pane collapses to an unusable width, and set `min-width: 0` so wide content cannot block resizing. Below a [breakpoint](node:Breakpoint), stack the panes or show one at a time.
quotes: The divider gets stuck whenever I drag over the preview.
The preview is an iframe, so the split pane loses the pointer. Disable its pointer events during the drag.

nodes.name: Masonry layout
nodes.description: A layout that packs items of uneven height into columns, placing each in the lane with the most room.
quotes: Tabbing through the gallery jumps from column to column.
That comes with the masonry layout. If order matters here, use a normal grid.

nodes.name: Aspect ratio
nodes.description: The proportion between an element's width and height, used to reserve space and keep media from distorting.
nodes.markdown:
An aspect ratio is the proportion between an element's width and height, such as 16:9 for video or 1:1 for a square thumbnail. In CSS, the `aspect-ratio` property lets the browser calculate one dimension from the other. Its most frequent job is reserving space, so the page does not jump when an image finishes loading and pushes the text below it down.

```css
.thumbnail {
  width: 100%;
  aspect-ratio: 16 / 9;
  object-fit: cover;
}
```

For images, set the `width` and `height` attributes in HTML as well. Browsers use them to work out the ratio before the file arrives, so layout space is reserved early, even when CSS sets `width: 100%` and `height: auto`.

When the media does not match the box, `object-fit` decides what happens.

| Value     | Result                            | Use                    |
| --------- | --------------------------------- | ---------------------- |
| `fill`    | Stretches, distorting the image   | Rarely                 |
| `cover`   | Fills the box, cropping the edges | Thumbnails, [avatars](node:Avatar) |
| `contain` | Fits inside, leaving empty bands  | Logos, product photos  |

Content taller than the box is the usual surprise. An element with `aspect-ratio` has an automatic minimum height based on its content, so a [card](node:Card) set to 1:1 grows past square when its text is long. The ratio appears to be ignored. Setting `overflow: auto` or `hidden` makes the element a scroll container, which removes that minimum and keeps the ratio. Setting `min-height: 0` also keeps the ratio, but content then overflows unless you handle it separately.

Forcing text into a fixed ratio carries an accessibility risk. Users who enlarge text need the box to grow, and WCAG 1.4.4 Resize Text does not allow clipped content at 200 percent. Apply fixed ratios to media and let text containers keep their automatic height.

An explicit `width` and `height` together override the ratio, because both dimensions are already known. Set only one when you want the ratio to apply.
quotes: The article list jumps around as the thumbnails load.
The images have no dimensions. Set an aspect ratio so the space is reserved.

nodes.name: Safe area
nodes.description: The part of a screen not covered by notches, rounded corners or system bars, where content stays fully visible.
nodes.markdown:
A safe area is the part of a screen not covered by notches, rounded corners or system bars, where content stays fully visible. A fixed bottom bar whose buttons sit under the phone's home indicator, or text clipped by a camera cutout in landscape, is the usual sign that a page has ignored it.

CSS exposes the insets through environment variables, read with the `env()` function.

| Variable                   | Typical cause on a phone          |
| -------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| `safe-area-inset-top`      | Notch or status area              |
| `safe-area-inset-right`    | Cutout in landscape               |
| `safe-area-inset-bottom`   | Home indicator                    |
| `safe-area-inset-left`     | Cutout in landscape               |

On devices with cutouts, browsers generally keep the page inside the safe area by default. To draw edge to edge, a page opts in with `viewport-fit=cover`, and from then on it is responsible for keeping content clear of the unsafe regions.

```html
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1, viewport-fit=cover" />
```

```css
.bottom-bar {
  position: fixed;
  inset-inline: 0;
  bottom: 0;
  padding-block-end: max(0.75rem, env(safe-area-inset-bottom));
}
```

The `max()` keeps a minimum padding on devices where the inset is 0, which includes rectangular displays with nothing occupying the viewport. The second argument of `env()` is a fallback used when the variable is not available, as in `env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px)`.

Three mistakes are common. Adding `viewport-fit=cover` without using the insets puts content under the hardware. Padding only the bottom works in portrait, but rotating the device moves the cutout to a side, so the left and right insets matter as well. Offsetting a bar with `bottom: env(safe-area-inset-bottom)` instead of padding it leaves page content visible in the strip beneath.

[Bottom navigation](node:Bottom%20navigation), [bottom sheets](node:Bottom%20sheet), [toasts](node:Toast) and [floating buttons](node:Floating%20action%20button) are the components most often affected. Test them on a real device or simulator in both orientations, because a desktop browser usually reports an inset of 0.
quotes: The checkout button is partly under the iPhone home bar.
We set `viewport-fit=cover` but never added the safe area inset to the footer padding.

nodes.name: Breakpoint
nodes.description: A width at which a layout changes, usually written as a CSS media query.
nodes.markdown:
A breakpoint is a width at which a layout changes, such as a [sidebar](node:Sidebar) collapsing into a menu below 48rem. It is usually written as a CSS media query, a rule that applies only when the viewport meets a condition. Breakpoints are one part of responsive design, which adapts a page to the space available.

```css
.layout { display: grid; gap: 1rem; }

@media (width >= 48em) {
  .layout { grid-template-columns: 16rem 1fr; }
}
```

Choose breakpoints where the content starts to look wrong, instead of copying the dimensions of particular phones. Device sizes change, and a layout tuned to three popular screens can break at every width between them.

| Question                               | Tool                      |
| -------------------------------------- | ------------------------- |
| Does the page have room for a sidebar? | Media query               |
| Does this component's parent have room? | Container query          |
| Should this size scale smoothly?       | [Fluid typography](node:Fluid%20typography), `clamp()` |
| Should items wrap when they run out of room? | Flex or grid wrapping |

A container query responds to the size of an ancestor element instead of the viewport, which suits a [card](node:Card) that appears in both a wide page and a narrow sidebar.

Using `em` in media queries has a specific benefit. It resolves against the browser's initial font size, not the page's CSS, so a user who increases their default font size gets the narrower layout sooner, and text has room.

Browser zoom also triggers breakpoints, because zooming reduces the viewport's width in CSS pixels. A 1280px window at 400 percent is 320 CSS pixels wide, which is the width WCAG 1.4.10 Reflow tests. Anything hidden at a small breakpoint must stay available in another form, or zoomed desktop users lose it.

Boundary bugs are a common symptom. Pairing `max-width: 767px` with `min-width: 768px` leaves a gap at fractional widths such as 767.5px, where neither rule applies and the layout looks broken. Range syntax avoids it with `width < 48em` and `width >= 48em`.
quotes: The nav disappears completely at exactly one window size.
Our two breakpoints leave a gap at 767.5px. Use range syntax so they meet.

nodes.name: Spacing scale
nodes.description: A fixed set of allowed spacing values used for padding, margins and gaps across an interface.
nodes.markdown:
A spacing scale is a fixed set of allowed values for padding, margins and gaps across an interface. Instead of choosing 13px here and 17px there, developers pick the nearest step. Without one, a product drifts into dozens of nearly identical values, and screens look slightly misaligned even though no single rule is wrong.

Many scales build on a base of 4 or 8 pixels, with steps that grow as the values get larger.

| Name         | Value     | Pixels at default | Typical use                 |
| ------------ | --------- | ----------------- | --------------------------- |
| `--space-1`  | `0.25rem` | 4                 | Icon and label              |
| `--space-2`  | `0.5rem`  | 8                 | Inside compact controls     |
| `--space-3`  | `0.75rem` | 12                | Control padding             |
| `--space-4`  | `1rem`    | 16                | Between related fields      |
| `--space-6`  | `1.5rem`  | 24                | [Card](node:Card) padding                |
| `--space-8`  | `2rem`    | 32                | Between groups              |
| `--space-12` | `3rem`    | 48                | Between page sections       |

Publish the values as CSS variables or design tokens, which are named design values shared across code and design files. Naming each step by its multiple of the base, as above, leaves room to add a value later without renaming everything. Names like `small` and `medium` run out quickly.

```css
.card {
  display: grid;
  gap: var(--space-3);
  padding: var(--space-6);
}
```

Use spacing to show relationships. Items that belong together get a smaller gap than items that do not, so a label sits closer to its own input than to the previous field. When every gap is the same, grouping is lost and forms become harder to scan.

Reduce large section spacing on narrow screens at a [breakpoint](node:Breakpoint).

The common failure is erosion through one-off values added to fix a single screen. Lint for raw pixel values in spacing properties, and add a new step only when several components need it. A [stack layout](node:Stack%20layout) that takes a scale value as its gap keeps these decisions in one place.
quotes: Why is this form 15px apart when the other one is 16?
Someone hard-coded it. Use the spacing scale so they stay consistent.

nodes.name: Type scale
nodes.description: A limited, related set of font sizes that gives text a consistent hierarchy across an interface.
nodes.markdown:
A type scale is a limited, related set of font sizes that gives text a consistent hierarchy across an interface. Without a scale, a product collects sizes like 15px, 16px and 17px that are too close to read as different levels and too numerous to maintain.

A common way to build one is to multiply a base size by a fixed ratio. The table uses a base of `1rem` and a ratio of 1.25, rounded to three decimals.

| Step      | Size       | Pixels at default | Line height | Use            |
| --------- | ---------- | ----------------- | ----------- | -------------- |
| `small`   | `0.8rem`   | 12.8              | 1.5         | Captions       |
| `base`    | `1rem`     | 16                | 1.5         | Body text      |
| `lg`      | `1.25rem`  | 20                | 1.4         | Lead text      |
| `xl`      | `1.563rem` | 25                | 1.3         | [Card](node:Card) titles    |
| `2xl`     | `1.953rem` | 31.25             | 1.2         | Section titles |
| `3xl`     | `2.441rem` | 39                | 1.1         | Page titles    |

A larger ratio creates stronger contrast between levels and suits marketing pages. A smaller ratio suits dense dashboards, where big headings would waste space. Define line height with each size, since large text generally needs tighter leading than body text.

```css
:root {
  --text-base: 1rem;
  --text-xl: 1.563rem;
}
h2 { font-size: var(--text-xl); line-height: 1.3; }
```

Keep visual size separate from heading level. A common failure is choosing `<h4>` because it looks the right size, which breaks the outline that people using a screen reader, which reads the UI aloud, navigate by. Choose the heading level from the document's structure, then apply whichever scale step fits.

Use `rem` for font sizes. A size in `px` does not follow the default font size a user sets in their browser, although page zoom still works. Check that nothing clips when text grows, since WCAG 1.4.4 Resize Text requires text to resize to 200 percent without loss of content or function.

To adapt the scale to screen width, change its values at a [breakpoint](node:Breakpoint) or use [fluid typography](node:Fluid%20typography).
quotes: Our card titles and section headings look almost identical.
They're one pixel apart. Map both onto the type scale so they differ by a full step.

nodes.name: Fluid typography
nodes.description: Text that scales smoothly with the viewport between a minimum and maximum size, usually using clamp().
nodes.markdown:
Fluid typography is text that scales smoothly with the viewport between a minimum and a maximum size, instead of jumping at a [breakpoint](node:Breakpoint). It is usually written with the CSS `clamp()` function, which takes a minimum, a preferred value and a maximum.

```css
h1 {
  font-size: clamp(1.5rem, 1rem + 2.5vw, 3rem);
}
```

The browser resolves `clamp(MIN, VAL, MAX)` as `max(MIN, min(VAL, MAX))`. In this example, the heading is `1.5rem` on small screens, `3rem` on large screens, and grows with the viewport in between.

| Approach                 | Behaviour                     | Suits                         |
| ------------------------ | ----------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| Fixed [type scale](node:Type%20scale) | Same at all widths | Dense application interfaces |
| Steps at breakpoints     | Jumps between sizes           | Simple, predictable control   |
| Fluid with `clamp()`     | Continuous between two limits | Headings, marketing pages     |

The main failure is text that does not respond to zoom. Browser zoom reduces the viewport's width in CSS pixels, so a size set only in `vw` stays about the same physical size however far the user zooms. WCAG lists this as failure F94 under 1.4.4 Resize Text, which requires text to be resizable to 200 percent without loss of content or functionality.

Mixing a `rem` value into the preferred value helps, because the `rem` part responds to zoom and to the user's font-size setting. It does not fully solve the problem, since the `vw` part still shrinks in CSS pixels as zoom increases, so the text grows by less than the zoom factor. MDN advises making the maximum a relative unit at least twice the minimum, so that text can still reach 200 percent. The example above follows that rule. Test it by zooming and comparing the rendered size.

Do not use `px` for the limits, since they ignore the user's default font size. Body text benefits least from fluid scaling, and a fixed `1rem` is often the better choice.
quotes: The hero title doesn't get any bigger when I zoom to 200 percent.
Its fluid typography is pure `vw`. Add a `rem` component and clamp it.

nodes.name: Elevation
nodes.description: The apparent height of a surface above the page, shown with shadow or tone to communicate layering.
quotes: In high contrast mode the dropdown blends into the page.
Its elevation is only a box shadow, which gets removed. Add a transparent border.

nodes.name: Theming
nodes.description: Changing an interface's visual values, such as colors and radii, by swapping named variables without editing components.
quotes: The date popup stays light inside our dark sidebar.
It's portalled out of the theming scope. Pass the `data-theme` attribute to the portal root.

nodes.name: Dark mode
nodes.description: An alternate color theme with light text on dark surfaces, following a system preference or a user choice.
nodes.markdown:
Dark mode is an alternate color theme with light text on dark surfaces, following a system preference or a user's choice. It is a specific case of [theming](node:Theming), and it takes more than inverting colors. A page that flashes white on every load, or a dark page with a bright white scrollbar and date input, is a sign that only some of the required parts were done.

Three CSS features handle different jobs.

| Feature                 | Job                                                     |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| `prefers-color-scheme`  | Detects the user's system preference                    |
| `color-scheme`          | Tells the browser to render native UI in light or dark  |
| `light-dark()`          | Picks one of two values based on the used color scheme  |

The `color-scheme` property affects the canvas, scrollbars, form controls and system colors. It is also required for `light-dark()` to work.

```css
:root { color-scheme: light dark; }

body {
  background: light-dark(#ffffff, #16181d);
  color: light-dark(#1a1a1a, #e8e8e8);
}
```

```html
<meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark" />
```

The meta tag gives the browser the preference before CSS loads, which helps prevent a white flash. If the app offers its own toggle, provide three options: System, Light and Dark. Store the choice, and apply it with a small inline script in `<head>` before the body paints. Setting `color-scheme: dark` on the root for the Dark option keeps native controls in step.

Colors need to be designed for dark surfaces, not flipped. Pure white on pure black can feel harsh, so many palettes soften both ends. Saturated brand colors that work on white may fall below the 4.5:1 text contrast ratio required by WCAG 1.4.3 on a dark background, so check every pair in both themes.

Shadows lose their effect, so show [elevation](node:Elevation) with lighter surfaces or borders. Logos with dark transparent backgrounds need an alternate asset.

Dark mode is separate from forced colors mode, an accessibility setting where the user's palette replaces page colors. Test both.
quotes: Dark mode looks fine except the scrollbars and select menus are bright white.
We never set `color-scheme`, so the browser still renders native controls in light.

nodes.name: Component library
nodes.description: A versioned collection of reusable UI components that teams install and build products from.
nodes.markdown:
A component library is a versioned collection of reusable UI pieces, such as [buttons](node:Button), inputs and dialogs, that teams install and build products from. It gives several applications one implementation of each control, so a fix to a [modal dialog](node:Modal%20dialog) reaches all of them. A design system, the wider set of standards, guidance and shared design decisions, may include a component library, but the library is only its code.

| Approach             | You get                         | You give up                    |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| Styled library       | Fast start, finished visuals    | Distinct look, easy overrides  |
| [Headless](node:Headless%20component) library | Behaviour and accessibility | You write all the styling |
| Copied-in source     | Full control of the code        | Upstream fixes arrive manually |
| Built in-house       | Exact fit                       | Ongoing maintenance cost       |

Controls such as a [combobox](node:Combobox) or [date picker](node:Date%20picker) are expensive to build well, so many teams adopt a tested library for them.

A breaking change can affect every consuming app at once, so follow semantic versioning: major for breaking changes, minor for additions, patch for fixes. Publish a changelog, deprecate an API before removing it. When upgrades become painful, teams stop taking them, and different apps end up pinned to different versions.

Style overrides are the other recurring problem. If consumers reach into internal class names to adjust a component, every internal change can break them. Expose supported options such as a [variant](node:Variant), CSS variables or a [slot](node:Slot), and treat the internal markup as private.

Using a library does not make a product accessible by itself. It can provide correct roles and keyboard support, but labels, heading order, focus destinations and color choices remain the product team's responsibility.

Document each component in a [component explorer](node:Component%20explorer) with its states, so teams can find what already exists before building a second version.
quotes: We've got four different date pickers across our apps.
Put one in the component library and migrate them over one at a time.

nodes.name: Primitive component
nodes.description: A low-level building block with a narrow job, from which larger components in a library are assembled.
nodes.markdown:
A primitive component is a low-level building block with one narrow job, from which larger components are assembled. Text, Box, Icon and a bare [button](node:Button) are typical examples. A `SearchBar` is not a primitive, because it combines several parts for a specific purpose. The term is used in two ways, which can confuse a conversation. | Meaning | Provides | Examples | | ------------------- | -------------------------------- | ---------------------------- | | Visual primitive | Styling and layout from tokens | Box, Text, [Stack](node:Stack%20layout) | | Behaviour primitive | State, keyboard and accessibility wiring | Dialog, Menu, [Tabs](node:Tabs) parts | A behaviour primitive is usually a [headless component](node:Headless%20component) with no visual styling. In [atomic design](node:Atomic%20design), visual primitives roughly correspond to atoms. A primitive has to stay open, because it does not know where it will be used. It should forward standard attributes, event handlers and refs (handles to the underlying DOM node) to the element it renders. If it drops them, consumers cannot attach an `aria-describedby`, a test ID or a focus call, and they end up writing a replacement. ```jsx function Text({ as: Tag = "span", size = "base", className = "", ...rest }) { return ; } ``` Spreading `...rest` is what passes those attributes through. The `as` prop makes it a [polymorphic component](node:Polymorphic%20component), so the same text styles can apply to a `

` or `

` without changing the document's structure. The common failure is a primitive that accumulates options. A Box gains props for every CSS property, then responsive versions of each, until it is a second styling language. Keep props limited to values from your tokens, and let unusual cases use regular CSS. The opposite failure is promoting a component too early. A shape that appears twice may be coincidence, and a shared abstraction forces both uses to change together. Extract a primitive once several components need the same behaviour. A change to a primitive affects everything built on it, so it needs visual regression tests and a careful release.
quotes: I can't add `aria-describedby` to our Input.
The primitive component isn't forwarding extra props. Spread them onto the native element.

nodes.name: Headless component
nodes.description: A component that supplies behaviour, state and accessibility wiring but no visual styling.
nodes.markdown:
A headless component supplies behaviour, state and accessibility wiring but no visual styling. It handles things like opening a menu, tracking the active item and managing keyboard input, while you provide the styling. Teams choose one when a styled library's appearance would need constant overriding, but they do not want to rebuild a complex control such as a [combobox](node:Combobox) from scratch. | Option | Behaviour | Styling | Suits | | ----------------------------- | --------- | ------------ | ------------------------------ | | Styled [component library](node:Component%20library) | Included | Included | Internal tools, fast starts | | Headless component | Included | Yours | Products with their own design | | Built from scratch | Yours | Yours | Unusual interactions | Headless APIs usually come in one of two forms. Some ship unstyled parts as a [compound component](node:Compound%20component). Others ship a hook, or a function that returns attributes for you to spread on your own elements. ```jsx function Disclosure({ title, children }) { const { buttonProps, panelProps } = useDisclosure(); return ( <>
{children}
); } ``` Here, `buttonProps` would hold `aria-expanded`, `aria-controls` and a click handler, so the consumer never writes them. The usual way this breaks is a consumer dropping those props or spreading them on the wrong element. The control still looks correct while keyboard behaviour and screen reader output (the UI read aloud) stop working. A `
` given the [button](node:Button)'s props, for example, may lack focus and key handling. A headless library handles only part of accessibility. You remain responsible for visible labels, a [focus ring](node:Focus%20ring) with sufficient contrast, [touch target](node:Touch%20target) sizes, color contrast, [reduced motion](node:Reduced%20motion) and hover and selected styles. An unstyled menu can have correct accessibility attributes and still have no visible indication of which item is focused. Styling hooks matter when choosing a library. Good ones expose state through data attributes such as `data-state="open"`, so CSS can respond without extra logic. Check that it lets you control where an overlay renders, because a [portal](node:Portal) can affect [theming](node:Theming) and stacking.
quotes: Should we write our own select so it matches the brand?
No. Use a headless component for the keyboard and ARIA behaviour and style it ourselves.

nodes.name: Compound component
nodes.description: A set of components designed to work together, sharing state implicitly through a common parent.
nodes.markdown:
A compound component is a set of components designed to work together, sharing state implicitly through a common parent. The HTML `<select>` and `<option>` elements work this way: neither is useful alone, and the parent tracks which option is chosen. In a [component library](node:Component%20library), the same idea looks like this:

```jsx
<Tabs defaultValue="account">
  <Tabs.List>
    <Tabs.Trigger value="account">Account</Tabs.Trigger>
    <Tabs.Trigger value="billing">Billing</Tabs.Trigger>
  </Tabs.List>
  <Tabs.Panel value="account"><AccountForm /></Tabs.Panel>
  <Tabs.Panel value="billing"><BillingForm /></Tabs.Panel>
</Tabs>
```

The alternative is a single component configured with data, such as `<Tabs items={[...]} />`. That API is shorter, but it struggles once one tab needs a [badge](node:Badge), another needs a [tooltip](node:Tooltip) and a third needs a different wrapper. Each request adds another prop, and the component ends up with options like `renderTabLabel` and `tabClassNameByIndex`.

| API style       | Good for                        | Weakness                    |
| --------------- | ------------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| Config prop     | Uniform, data-driven lists      | Grows a prop per exception  |
| Compound        | Flexible structure and content  | More verbose to use         |
| [Render prop](node:Render%20prop) | Custom output from internal state | Harder to read when nested |
| [Slot](node:Slot) | Replacing named regions       | Fixed set of regions        |

The parent usually shares state through a context, a framework feature that passes data to descendants without props. Older implementations used `cloneElement` to inject props into direct children. That approach breaks as soon as someone wraps a child in a `<div>` or their own component, and the tab silently stops responding. Context works at any depth, so prefer it.

A part rendered outside its parent has no context to read. Throw a clear error such as "Tabs.Trigger must be used within Tabs" rather than failing with an undefined value.

Accessibility wiring is a major benefit of this pattern. The parent can generate IDs and connect `aria-controls`, `aria-labelledby` and `aria-selected` across parts, and it can run [roving tabindex](node:Roving%20tabindex) so the caller never handles them.
quotes: Our Tabs component has 22 props now, mostly for one-off tab labels.
Make it a compound component so callers can put whatever they need inside each trigger.

nodes.name: Polymorphic component
nodes.description: A component that can render as different HTML elements or components, usually through an as prop.
nodes.markdown:
A polymorphic component can render as different HTML elements or components, usually through a prop named `as`. It lets the same styles apply to different semantics. A `Button` can render a `<button>` for an action and an `<a>` for navigation while looking identical.

```jsx
function Button({ as: Tag = "button", ...props }) {
  const typeProp = Tag === "button" ? { type: "button" } : {};
  return <Tag className="btn" {...typeProp} {...props} />;
}

<Button onClick={save}>Save</Button>
<Button as="a" href="/pricing">See pricing</Button>
```

Pick the element that matches the behaviour. A link navigates to a URL, and a button performs an action. Changing the tag changes what the browser provides, and the component does not get that behaviour back for free.

| Rendered as      | What changes                                                     |
| ---------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `<button>`       | Focusable, activates on Enter and Space, supports `disabled`     |
| `<a href>`       | Focusable, activates on Enter only, can open in a new tab        |
| `<a>` no `href`  | Not a link and not focusable                                     |
| `<div>`          | No role, no focus, no keyboard activation                        |

Using `as="div"` on an interactive component removes its keyboard behaviour. It still looks and clicks like a button, but keyboard users cannot reach it and screen readers, which read the UI aloud, do not announce it as a control. Restrict the allowed values, or add the role, `tabindex` and key handling when a non-interactive element is truly required.

Attributes do not all carry over either. `disabled` has no effect on an `<a>`, so a "disabled" link stays clickable. If a link must appear unavailable, remove the `href` and communicate the [disabled state](node:Disabled%20state) another way.

TypeScript adds cost. Correctly typing props that change with `as` requires complex generics, which can slow the type checker and produce hard-to-read errors. An alternative is the `asChild` pattern, where the component merges its props onto a single child element supplied by the caller, as described in [Slot](node:Slot). This leaves the choice of element visible in the calling code and avoids the generic types.
quotes: The nav item looks like a button but Tab skips it.
Someone passed `as="div"` to our polymorphic component. It should be an anchor with an `href`.

nodes.name: Slot
nodes.description: A named placeholder inside a component where the caller supplies their own content.
nodes.markdown:
A slot is a named placeholder inside a component where the caller supplies their own content. The component controls the structure and position, and the caller controls what goes there. A `Card` might expose `header`, `media` and `footer` slots. Slots usually replace a growing list of props such as `title`, `titleIcon`, `titleColor` and `subtitle`, each added for one screen. ```jsx function Card({ header, footer, children }) { return (
{header}
{children}
{footer &&
{footer}
}
); } Invoice 1042} footer={}> Due on 14 March ``` The mechanism differs by technology. | Technology | How a slot is expressed | | -------------- | ------------------------------------------ | | Web Components | `` in the shadow tree | | Vue | `` in the template | | React | `children` and props that accept elements | In Web Components, a `` can contain fallback content, shown when nothing is assigned to it. Slotted nodes remain in the light DOM, the host's regular children, and are only displayed at the slot's position. Page styles therefore still apply to them, and `::slotted()` from inside the component reaches only the top-level assigned elements. Some libraries use the word for a different technique. An `asChild` prop, or a `Slot` utility, merges a component's props onto the single element the caller passes, so a menu trigger can be a custom link without an extra wrapper. This fails when the child does not pass received props and refs to its DOM node, leaving the trigger inert. Slots hand structure to callers, which brings accessibility risk. A caller can put a link inside a slot that is already wrapped in a [button](node:Button), producing invalid nested interactive content. Document what each slot accepts, and wire names from the component, for example by connecting a dialog's title slot through `aria-labelledby`. Prefer a slot when content varies. Use a plain prop for simple data like a label string, and a [render prop](node:Render%20prop) when the content depends on the component's internal state.
quotes: Design wants an icon and a link in the card title now.
Stop adding title props. Give the card a header slot.

nodes.name: Render prop
nodes.description: A prop whose value is a function that the component calls with internal state to produce UI.
nodes.markdown:
A render prop is a prop whose value is a function that the component calls with its internal state to produce UI. The component owns the logic, and the caller decides what the output looks like. It is useful when the content of a region depends on data only the component knows, such as which row is being rendered in a list. ```jsx ( )} /> ``` The nearest alternatives solve slightly different problems. | Pattern | Content depends on internal state | Typical use | | ------------------- | --------------------------------- | -------------------------- | | [Slot](node:Slot) | No | Fixed regions of a layout | | Render prop | Yes | List items, custom cells | | Hook | Yes, caller owns all markup | Sharing logic only | | [Compound component](node:Compound%20component) | Via context | Multi-part widgets | In React, hooks replaced many earlier uses of render props for sharing logic, because several render props combined produced deeply nested callbacks. The pattern remains a good fit when a parent must render per item, as a [virtualized list](node:Virtualized%20list) or [data table](node:Data%20table) does when it asks the caller how to draw each row. Performance is the first thing that goes wrong. An inline function has a new identity on every render, so a memoized child that receives it re-renders each time. Memoize the row component itself, and keep the function stable if measurements show a problem. Remounting is a less obvious failure. Defining a component inside the render function creates a new component type on each render, so the framework discards the previous subtree. Inputs lose their text and focus disappears. Return elements of a stable component type instead. Render props can also drop accessibility wiring, because the caller writes the markup. If the component needs `role`, `id` or `aria-selected` on each option, pass them as a props object, and require the caller to spread it, as in `renderOption={(option, props) =>
  • {option.label}
    • }`.
quotes: Every keystroke in the row's input loses focus.
The render prop defines a new component inline, so it remounts. Move it out.

nodes.name: Variant
nodes.description: A named, predefined visual version of a component, selected through a prop such as primary or danger.
nodes.markdown:
A variant is a named, predefined visual version of a component, selected through a prop such as `variant="danger"`. Variants give a [component library](node:Component%20library) a limited set of approved appearances, so teams do not restyle a [button](node:Button) with one-off classes on each screen.

```jsx
<Button variant="primary" size="md">Save</Button>
<Button variant="danger" size="sm">Delete</Button>
```

A component's styling usually has separate axes, and each should be its own prop.

| Axis     | Example values               | Describes                     |
| -------- | ---------------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| Variant  | `primary`, `secondary`, `ghost` | Visual emphasis            |
| Tone     | `neutral`, `danger`, `success`  | Meaning                    |
| Size     | `sm`, `md`, `lg`             | Physical scale                |
| State    | hover, focus, disabled       | Current interaction, not a prop choice |

Interaction states are not variants. A [hover state](node:Hover%20state) or [disabled state](node:Disabled%20state) applies on top of every variant, so each one has to be designed and tested for all of them.

Use a union value instead of boolean props. With `<Button primary danger ghost>`, the API allows contradictory combinations and nothing says which wins. A single `variant` prop with a closed set of values makes invalid combinations impossible, and a type checker can enforce it.

Combinations are the main cost. Three variants, three tones, three sizes and five states already produce 135 possible appearances. Some will be unintended or untested, and a danger ghost button may fail contrast even though the other pairings pass. Define only the combinations you support, and list them in a [component explorer](node:Component%20explorer) so that gaps are visible. Each one must meet the 4.5:1 text contrast of WCAG 1.4.3, and its [focus ring](node:Focus%20ring) must remain visible.

A `danger` button also needs a label that states the action, because color alone does not convey meaning.

If a new option changes behaviour, structure or required props, it is probably a separate component.
quotes: Can I just add a red class to this button?
Use the danger variant so it gets the tested hover, focus and contrast styles.

nodes.name: Uncontrolled component
nodes.description: A component that keeps its own state internally, taking only an initial value from its parent.
nodes.markdown:
An uncontrolled component keeps its own state internally and takes only an initial value from its parent. A plain HTML `<input>` works this way: the browser stores what the user types, and your code reads it when needed. The opposite is a controlled component, where the parent owns the value and passes it down on every change.

```jsx
// Uncontrolled: the DOM holds the value
<input name="email" defaultValue={user.email} />

// Controlled: the parent holds the value
<input value={email} onChange={(e) => setEmail(e.target.value)} />
```

| Question                                 | Uncontrolled          | Controlled        |
| ---------------------------------------- | --------------------- | ----------------- |
| Where is the value stored?               | DOM or component      | Parent state      |
| Read the value only on submit?           | A good fit            | Extra code        |
| Validate or format on each keystroke?    | Awkward               | A good fit        |
| Keep two views in sync?                  | Difficult             | A good fit        |
| Re-render on each keystroke?             | No                    | Usually           |

Uncontrolled [text fields](node:Text%20field) suit simple forms, because `FormData` can collect every named field at submit time and the parent does not re-render while the user types.

A common bug comes from expecting the initial value to update. `defaultValue` is read only when the component first mounts. If a user switches from customer A to customer B and the same form stays mounted, the fields still show customer A's data. Giving the form a key tied to the record forces a fresh mount:

```jsx
<CustomerForm key={customer.id} customer={customer} />
```

Another common failure is switching modes. In React, a `value` that starts as `undefined` and later becomes a string turns an uncontrolled input into a controlled one and logs a warning. Initialise the state to an empty string, or use `value ?? ""`. A `value` with no `onChange` handler produces a field that cannot be edited.

Library components often support both modes, accepting `value` with `onChange`, or `defaultValue` alone. A [dropdown menu](node:Dropdown%20menu) may have `open` and `defaultOpen`, for example. Follow this naming so callers can start uncontrolled and take over the state only when they need it.
quotes: The edit form still shows the last customer after I pick a new one.
It's an uncontrolled component using `defaultValue`. Add a `key` so it remounts.

nodes.name: Component explorer
nodes.description: A development tool that renders components in isolation so each state can be built, reviewed and tested.
nodes.markdown:
A component explorer is a development tool that renders components in isolation, so each state can be built, reviewed and tested without running the full application. Storybook is a widely used example. Reaching a payment form's declined message in the real app might take a login, a seeded account and a failed card, whereas an explorer shows that state directly.

Each entry, often called a story, renders a component with fixed inputs.

| State to capture  | Why it is worth having                     |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| Default           | Baseline for review                        |
| Loading           | Shows the [skeleton screen](node:Skeleton%20screen) or [spinner](node:Spinner) |
| [Empty state](node:Empty%20state) | Rarely seen during normal development |
| [Error state](node:Error%20state) | Hard to trigger in the real app   |
| Long content      | Exposes overflow and truncation            |
| Dark theme        | Exposes hard-coded colors                  |

Designers can review real components in a browser, and generated prop tables turn the explorer into documentation for a [component library](node:Component%20library).

It also provides a base for automated tests. Visual regression tools compare screenshots of each story to catch unintended changes, and automated accessibility checkers can run against each state. These checkers find only some issues, so manual testing with a keyboard and a screen reader (software that reads the UI aloud) is still needed.

Stories go out of date when they are written once and abandoned. Run them as tests in continuous integration so that a broken story fails the build.

Isolation also hides integration problems. A component can look correct in an explorer and break in the app, because the app adds global CSS, providers, real data lengths or a parent that creates a stacking context, which traps `z-index` values. Load the application's global styles and providers in the explorer and use realistic data.
quotes: How do I see the payment form's declined state without a test card?
Open it in the component explorer. There's a story for each error.

nodes.name: Atomic design
nodes.description: A methodology by Brad Frost that describes interfaces in five levels, from atoms up to complete pages.
nodes.markdown:
Atomic design is a methodology created by Brad Frost that describes interfaces in five levels, from small parts up to complete pages. It borrows its names from chemistry. Its purpose is to help a team think about an interface as a whole and as a collection of parts at the same time.

| Level     | Definition                                  | Example                  |
| --------- | ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------ |
| Atoms     | Basic elements that cannot be reduced further and still function | Label, input, [button](node:Button) |
| Molecules | Simple groups of atoms working as one unit  | [Search field](node:Search%20field) |
| Organisms | Distinct sections built from smaller parts  | Site header              |
| Templates | Page layouts showing content structure      | Article layout           |
| Pages     | Templates filled with representative content | The real pricing page   |

The page level is useful because a headline that fits a template with placeholder text may wrap to four lines with a real title. In code, atoms roughly correspond to a [primitive component](node:Primitive%20component).

Frost describes atomic design as a mental model and states that it is not a linear process.

The common failure comes from applying the levels as a strict folder structure. A team creates `atoms/`, `molecules/` and `organisms/`, then spends review time arguing about whether a [card](node:Card) is a molecule or an organism. The answer rarely affects how the code works. Many teams organise files by feature or component name and keep the vocabulary for discussion only.

The hierarchy says nothing about accessibility on its own. A set of accessible atoms can still form an inaccessible organism, for example if a label is separated from its input or the heading levels are wrong when the parts combine. Test at the level where users actually meet the interface.
quotes: Is this filter bar a molecule or an organism?
It doesn't matter. Atomic design is there to help us talk about it, so put it with the search feature.

nodes.name: Hover state
nodes.description: The visual change on an element while a pointer rests over it, signalling that it can be interacted with.
quotes: How do I delete a row on the iPad? I can't see the button.
It only appears in the hover state. Show the actions when the device can't hover.

nodes.name: Focus ring
nodes.description: The visible outline showing which element currently has keyboard focus.
nodes.markdown:
A focus ring is the visible outline showing which element currently has keyboard focus. A stylesheet containing `outline: none` with no replacement is a common failure: pressing Tab appears to do nothing, because focus is moving through the page invisibly.

Three WCAG 2.2 criteria apply.

| Criterion                     | Level | Requirement                                                       |
| ----------------------------- | ----- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 2.4.7 Focus Visible           | AA    | A visible indicator exists in keyboard use                        |
| 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast      | AA    | A custom indicator has 3:1 contrast against adjacent colors       |
| 2.4.13 Focus Appearance       | AAA   | At least the area of a 2px perimeter, with 3:1 change between the focused and unfocused states |

Use `:focus-visible`, which applies when the browser judges that focus should be shown. It shows the ring for keyboard navigation and for text inputs, and generally omits it on mouse clicks of [buttons](node:Button).

```css
:focus-visible {
  outline: 2px solid var(--color-focus);
  outline-offset: 2px;
}
```

Prefer `outline` over `box-shadow` for the ring. Forced colors mode, an accessibility setting that replaces page colors with a user palette, sets `box-shadow` to `none`, so a shadow-only ring disappears. Outlines stay and take on a system color.

One color rarely works on every surface. A blue ring can vanish on a blue button or a dark panel. Either set the color per [theme](node:Theming), or draw a two-tone ring using an outline plus a contrasting inner shadow, so that one of the two always stands out.

Clipping is the other frequent bug. An ancestor with `overflow: hidden` cuts off the outer part of the ring, which shows up on items in scroll containers and on [cards](node:Card). Use a negative `outline-offset` to draw the ring inside the element. A [sticky header](node:Sticky%20header) can also cover the focused element entirely, which fails WCAG 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum), and `scroll-padding` prevents that.
quotes: I can't tell where I am when I tab through the settings page.
A CSS reset removed the outline. Add a focus ring with `:focus-visible`.

nodes.name: Active state
nodes.description: The brief visual change on a control while it is being pressed, confirming that the input registered.
nodes.markdown:
An active state is the brief visual change on a control while it is being pressed, confirming that the input registered. In CSS it is written with `:active`, which with a mouse typically begins on press and ends on release. A [button](node:Button) with no pressed feedback can feel unresponsive, and people often click it a second time.

The word "active" is also used loosely for a persistent state.

| Term             | Meaning                         | How to express it                 |
| ---------------- | ------------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| Active (pressed) | Being pressed right now         | `:active`                         |
| Toggled on       | A [toggle button](node:Toggle%20button) stays on | `aria-pressed="true"` |
| Current page     | Where the user is in navigation | `aria-current="page"`             |
| Selected         | Chosen item in a set            | `aria-selected="true"`            |

A nav link styled with `:active` will not stay highlighted on the current page, because the pseudo-class ends on release. Use `aria-current="page"` and style from that attribute, which also tells screen readers (software that reads the UI aloud) which link is current.

```css
.button:hover { background: var(--accent-hover); }
.button:active { background: var(--accent-pressed); }
```

A later `:hover` rule with equal specificity overrides `:active`, so the pressed style never shows while the pointer is over the element. For links, declare the rules in the order `:link`, `:visited`, `:hover`, `:active`.

Moving the control on press can lose the click. If `:active` applies `transform: translateY(2px)` and the user presses near the top edge, the button slides from under the pointer. The release then lands on another element, and the browser fires `click` on their common ancestor, so the button's handler does not run. Apply the movement to an inner element, or use a color or a slight shadow change.

Browsers differ on whether `:active` matches during keyboard or touch activation, so do not make it the only feedback for an action. Under [reduced motion](node:Reduced%20motion), limit press effects to color changes.
quotes: The current nav item only highlights while I'm clicking it.
You've used the active state. Set `aria-current="page"` and style that instead.

nodes.name: Disabled state
nodes.description: A control shown but currently unavailable, with its interaction blocked until a condition changes.
nodes.markdown:
A disabled state shows a control that exists but is currently unavailable, with interaction blocked until a condition changes. A greyed-out Submit [button](node:Button) is the familiar case, and also the familiar complaint: the user cannot tell why it is grey or what would enable it. HTML offers `disabled`, and ARIA (attributes for assistive technology) offers `aria-disabled`. They behave differently. | Behaviour | `disabled` | `aria-disabled="true"` | | ------------------- | ---------------------- | --------------------------------- | | In the Tab order | No | Yes | | Blocks activation | Yes | No, your code must block it | | Automatic styles | Yes, via `:disabled` | No, style the attribute | | Submitted in forms | No | Yes, handle it yourself | | Works on any element | Form controls only | Any element with a suitable role | The WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices advise using `disabled` when users can infer the control from what is around it, such as Previous on the first page of results. Use `aria-disabled` when the control should remain discoverable, such as items in a [toolbar](node:Toolbar) or menu, since people using a screen reader, which reads the UI aloud, find content largely by moving focus. ```html

Add a title before publishing.

``` With `aria-disabled`, block both click and keyboard activation in script. `pointer-events: none` stops the mouse only. Often it is better not to disable the control. Leave Submit enabled, and on click show what is missing with [inline validation](node:Inline%20validation) or an [error summary](node:Error%20summary). Native `disabled` has its own traps. If a focused button becomes disabled during a request, focus can be lost. A [tooltip](node:Tooltip) explaining the reason generally will not work on it either, because the button cannot receive focus and may not fire pointer events. Use `aria-disabled` when an explanation is needed. WCAG 1.4.3 and 1.4.11 exempt inactive components from contrast requirements, but keep the label readable so users know what the control is.
quotes: Why can't I click Publish? Nothing tells me.
It's in a disabled state until there's a title. Enable it and show the error on submit.

nodes.name: Touch target
nodes.description: The area of a control that accepts a tap or click, which can be larger than the visible icon or text.
nodes.markdown:
A touch target is the area of a control that accepts a tap or click, which can be larger than the visible icon or text. When it is too small, or too close to a neighbour, users tap the wrong item or need several attempts. A 16px close icon beside a Delete [button](node:Button) is the kind of layout that produces these errors, particularly for people with tremors or limited dexterity.

WCAG 2.2 has two criteria for size, and they are often confused. Both apply to all pointer input, including a mouse.

| Criterion                  | Level | Minimum size      | Spacing exception |
| -------------------------- | ----- | ----------------- | ----------------- |
| 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) | AA   | 24 by 24 CSS px   | Yes               |
| 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced) | AAA | 44 by 44 CSS px   | No                |

Under 2.5.8, a smaller target can still pass through spacing. Draw a 24px diameter circle centred on the target's bounding box. The target passes if its circle does not intersect another target or the circle of another undersized target.

Other exceptions apply to 2.5.8:

| Exception          | Example                                                |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| Equivalent         | Another compliant control on the page does the same job |
| Inline             | A link inside a sentence                               |
| User agent control | An unstyled native control                             |
| Essential          | Pins on a map where position carries meaning           |

Criterion 2.5.5 has similar exceptions for equivalent, inline, user agent and essential targets, but no spacing exception.

The visible element can stay small while the target grows. Add padding, or extend the hit area with a pseudo-element:

```css
.icon-button { position: relative; width: 1rem; height: 1rem; }
.icon-button::after {
  content: "";
  position: absolute;
  inset: -0.25rem;
}
```

Here a 16px icon gets a 24px target at the default font size. Check that expanded hit areas do not overlap, because the element painted on top then takes the tap. Dense [toolbars](node:Toolbar), [data table](node:Data%20table) row actions, [chip](node:Chip) remove buttons and [icon buttons](node:Icon%20button) often fall short.
quotes: People keep hitting Delete when they mean to hit Edit on mobile.
Those icons are 16px and touching. Give each a bigger touch target and some space between them.

nodes.name: Roving tabindex
nodes.description: A focus technique where one item in a group is tabbable and arrow keys move focus among the rest.
nodes.markdown:
Roving tabindex is a focus technique where only one item in a group is in the Tab order, and arrow keys move focus among the rest. It makes a composite widget, one control made of many focusable parts, behave as a single Tab stop. Without it, a [toolbar](node:Toolbar) with 20 [buttons](node:Button) takes 20 presses of Tab to get past. The WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices describe the steps. | Step | When | What happens | | ---- | ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------- | | 1 | Widget loads | One item gets `tabindex="0"`, the others `tabindex="-1"` | | 2 | Arrow key pressed | Current item is set to `-1`, next item is set to `0` | | 3 | Same key handler | Call `.focus()` on the new item | | 4 | User tabs away and back | Focus returns to the item holding `tabindex="0"` | ```html
``` The usual alternative is `aria-activedescendant`. | Technique | Real DOM focus | Scrolling | Typical use | | ----------------------- | ----------------- | ------------------- | ----------------------------- | | Roving tabindex | Moves to the item | Browser handles it | Toolbars, tabs, [tree views](node:Tree%20view) | | `aria-activedescendant` | Stays on container | You handle it | [Combobox](node:Combobox) with typing focus in the input | Use `aria-activedescendant` when focus must stay in a text input while the user moves through suggestions. A common bug is losing the Tab stop. If the item holding `tabindex="0"` is removed or disabled, no item in the group is tabbable, and the widget can no longer be reached by keyboard. Whenever items change, confirm that exactly one remains at `0`. If the focused item was removed, move focus to a neighbour. Decide whether arrows wrap at the ends, and support Home and End where the pattern calls for them. Do not trap Tab inside the group, because Tab should always leave the widget. Keep the visible [focus ring](node:Focus%20ring) on the current item.
quotes: It takes 14 tabs to get past the editor's formatting bar.
It needs roving tabindex, so the bar is one Tab stop and arrows move inside it.

nodes.name: Drag and drop
nodes.description: Moving an item by pressing it, carrying it with a pointer and releasing it over a target.
nodes.markdown:
Drag and drop is moving an item by pressing it, carrying it with a pointer and releasing it over a target. It is used to reorder lists, move [kanban board](node:Kanban%20board) [cards](node:Card) and add files to a [file upload](node:File%20upload). It should not be the only way to do something, because it is difficult or impossible for many people.

| Phase    | User action        | Interface response                        |
| -------- | ------------------ | ----------------------------------------- |
| Pick up  | Presses and moves  | Item lifts, valid targets are indicated   |
| Move     | Carries the item   | Insertion point shown, edges auto-scroll  |
| Drop     | Releases           | Item lands, result saved                  |
| Cancel   | Presses Escape     | Item returns to its origin                |

WCAG treats input methods separately. Under 2.5.7 Dragging Movements (AA), anything done by dragging must also be achievable with a single pointer without dragging, unless dragging is essential. A keyboard alternative alone does not meet this, because it has to work with clicks or taps. Under 2.1.1 Keyboard (A), the function also has to work from a keyboard. A "Move to" menu or Up and Down buttons cover both. Announce each result through a `role="status"` region.

| API                 | Good at                               | Limitation                         |
| ------------------- | ------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| HTML Drag and Drop  | Files, dragging between windows       | Limited styling, uneven touch support |
| Pointer Events      | Custom reordering, touch and mouse    | You build the behaviour            |

With the HTML API, a drop target that never fires `drop` is a common bug. An element only becomes a valid target if its `dragover` event is cancelled.

```js
zone.addEventListener("dragover", (event) => event.preventDefault());
```

With Pointer Events, touch drags can be cancelled when the browser decides to scroll instead, which fires `pointercancel`. Set `touch-action: none` on a dedicated drag handle, not the whole item, so that users can still scroll and pinch zoom the page.

Save the result [optimistically](node:Optimistic%20UI) and return the item to its origin if the request fails.
quotes: Reordering works with a mouse but the list just scrolls on my phone.
The drag and drop handle needs `touch-action: none`, or the browser takes over the gesture.

nodes.name: Micro-interaction
nodes.description: A small, contained response to a single user action, such as a switch sliding or a heart filling in.
quotes: Users keep double-clicking Copy because nothing seems to happen.
Add a micro-interaction that swaps the label to Copied, and announce it through a status region.

nodes.name: Easing
nodes.description: The curve that controls how an animation's speed changes between its start and end.
nodes.markdown:
Easing is the curve that controls how an animation's speed changes between its start and end. The same 200ms movement can feel abrupt, mechanical or smooth depending on the curve.

CSS provides keywords, each equivalent to a specific function.

| Keyword       | Equivalent                         | Common use                     |
| ------------- | ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| `linear`      | `cubic-bezier(0, 0, 1, 1)`         | [Spinners](node:Spinner), [progress bars](node:Progress%20bar), opacity |
| `ease`        | `cubic-bezier(0.25, 0.1, 0.25, 1)` | The CSS default                |
| `ease-in`     | `cubic-bezier(0.42, 0, 1, 1)`      | Elements leaving the screen    |
| `ease-out`    | `cubic-bezier(0, 0, 0.58, 1)`      | Elements entering the screen   |
| `ease-in-out` | `cubic-bezier(0.42, 0, 0.58, 1)`   | Elements moving across screen  |

The usual convention is to use `ease-out` for things that appear, because they respond right away and then settle. Use `ease-in` for things that leave. Using `ease-in` on an entrance is a common mistake: the slow start reads as lag right after the user clicks.

Beyond the keywords, three functions give finer control. `cubic-bezier()` defines a custom curve. Its x values must stay between 0 and 1, while its y values may go outside that range to create overshoot. `linear()` draws a curve through points, and `steps()` jumps in discrete stages.

```css
.popover {
  transition: transform 180ms cubic-bezier(0.34, 1.56, 0.64, 1);
}
```

The y value of 1.56 makes the element pass its target and settle back.

In a `@keyframes` animation, the timing function applies between each pair of keyframes, not across the whole animation. A three-keyframe animation with `ease-in-out` slows to a stop at the middle keyframe, which appears as a stutter. Remove the middle keyframe, or set a timing function per keyframe.

Easing does not make motion safe. A gently curved animation can still cause discomfort, so honour [reduced motion](node:Reduced%20motion) separately. Define a few named curves as CSS variables so that [micro-interactions](node:Micro-interaction) across the product feel related.
quotes: The dropdown feels laggy even though it's only 150ms.
It's using `ease-in`, so it starts slowly. Change the easing to `ease-out`.

nodes.name: Reduced motion
nodes.description: Honouring a user's system setting that asks for less non-essential animation.
nodes.markdown:
Reduced motion means honouring a user's system setting that asks for less non-essential animation. Large movement such as parallax, zooming and sliding panels can cause dizziness or nausea for people with vestibular disorders, so an animation that looks harmless to its author can make a page unusable for someone else. Browsers expose the setting through the `prefers-reduced-motion` media feature, with the values `no-preference` and `reduce`.

The setting does not require removing all animation. Replace large motion with a gentler effect, and keep feedback that carries information.

| Original effect             | Under reduced motion           |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| Page or panel slide         | Crossfade or instant change    |
| Zoom into a [lightbox](node:Lightbox) | Fade in               |
| Parallax                    | Static background              |
| Auto-rotating [carousel](node:Carousel) | No auto-rotation    |
| Smooth scroll to anchor     | Instant jump                   |
| [Spinner](node:Spinner) rotation | Slow opacity pulse        |

```css
.panel { transition: transform 300ms ease-out; }

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  .panel { transition: opacity 150ms linear; }
}
```

WCAG 2.3.3 Animation from Interactions (AAA) requires that motion triggered by interaction can be disabled unless it is essential. Color or opacity changes that do not alter perceived size, shape or position are outside its definition of motion. WCAG 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide (A) separately covers content that moves automatically for more than five seconds alongside other content. For 2.2.2, provide a visible pause control as well as the media query.

A blanket reset is a common shortcut, and it can break an interface.

```css
* { animation: none !important; transition: none !important; }
```

With no transition, the `transitionend` event never fires.
